docs.title: Evey
docs.text:
Evey is a server you run at home for your films, series, music and photos. You add your media and the people who will watch. For each playback, the file, the player and the server negotiate how the picture is delivered, with nothing to choose before pressing play.

Install Evey Try the demo

Beta, no numbered release yet Free software, AGPL-3.0 Demo: signs you in by itself (demo / demo)

What you need: an x86-64 computer or NAS with Docker, a folder with your media, and a free port. One container, one compose file, one command. Watch in any web browser, on a Chromecast, on Android phones and tablets, and on Android TV. The Android and Android TV apps are in testing and not on Google Play yet.

Home: the titles to resume, then your libraries row by row. A film page: artwork, age rating, ratings, synopsis and credits. The web player. In the bar: Watch Together, Cast, and the (i) that opens Stream info. The dashboard while two people watch: the picture, the device, Direct Play or Remux.

docs.title: For everyone at home
docs.text:
• One profile per person. Each profile keeps its own history, resume points, favourites and languages; a household usually shares one account.
  • Kids profiles. A kids profile opens without a code; leaving it for an adult profile asks for a four-digit PIN. A profile can carry a maximum age, enforced by the server: a title above it is never sent, not even as a download.
  • Pick up where you left off, on any device: resume points live on the server, not on the phone.
  • On the go. The Android app downloads a title to watch offline, for 30 days.
  • On the TV. Android TV signs in with Quick Connect: a code shown on the screen, typed or scanned from a phone or a computer already signed in. No password typed with a remote.
  • Together. Several people watch the same title at the same moment, each on their own device.

Music and photo libraries get the same treatment as films and series, on the web, on Android and on the TV. Apps and devices · Users, profiles and parental control

docs.title: How a file reaches the screen
docs.text:
Evey never asks you to pick a quality. Each time a title starts, the server chooses from three things: what the file contains, what this player can decode, and what this server can encode right now. It prefers, in this order:

  • Direct Play: the file as it is.
  • Remux: the same picture and sound in another file format, nothing re-encoded. MKVGo does it inside the server where it can, without starting an extra program for each playback; FFmpeg copies the tracks otherwise.
  • Transcode: only the tracks the device cannot play are re-encoded by FFmpeg, often just the audio.

The same film can go untouched to a TV and be re-encoded for an older phone. In the player, Stream info shows the plan actually served and why the file was not sent as it is. Admin → Dashboard shows the same for every viewer.

The first playback of the dashboard above, seen from the player. Remux: the file format changes, picture and sound are copied, and the last line says why the file could not be sent as it is.

How playback is decided · MKVGo in Evey

docs.title: One container, and the server measures itself
docs.text:
One compose file is the whole installation: no .env to write, no memory or CPU setting.

  • Database and search engine run inside the container, reachable only from it, with passwords generated on the first start.
  • The server never runs as root. It runs as the owner of your media folder when it can detect one, so that repairs can write.
  • Transcoding capacity is measured, not guessed. At a quiet moment the server times real encodes on the processor and on each graphics card you gave the container; a card counts only for what succeeded. When room runs short, a new playback gets a lower quality, or moves from a busy card to the processor. A start that cannot be served is refused with a message that names the reason: the server is full, it is still measuring itself, or the file is not ready.
  • Remote access opens when you give the server a public address, and stays closed otherwise.

Bringing your own database or search engine stays possible: Advanced deployments. Transcoding and server capacity

docs.title: What Evey does with your files
docs.text:
Your files. Removing a title or a library removes it from Evey, not from the disk. Evey writes into your media folders only for a repair you asked for, for a subtitle fetched through the API, and for a small probe file that checks the folder watcher still works; mount a library read-only and none of that happens. Media Health reads your MKV and WebM files and lists what it finds; a repair rewrites a file only on request, in a copy checked in full before it replaces the file, keeps the original by default, and every change is journaled. What cannot be repaired is reported and left as it is. Media health

Your data. The project runs no service that receives it: no account with us, no analytics, no crash reporting. The apps talk to your server and to nothing else we operate. What leaves your network: the server asks outside services for artwork and descriptions (The Movie Database, and cover art sources for music), and once in a while asks the image registry whether a newer build exists, which you can switch off. The database is dumped before every update that changes it. Privacy policy · Backups and updates

docs.title: Plugins are contained, not trusted
docs.text: A plugin is analysed before install; the administrator sees its findings and the permissions it asks for, and a new permission needs an explicit acknowledgement. It runs as its own process under a separate user, with no direct network access, and is stopped when it exceeds its memory, process or disk limit. How much the filesystem is confined depends on the host, and the Security Dashboard shows the sandbox mode actually in use. Plugins add metadata sources, notification channels, home sections and player overlays; themes restyle the interface. A plugin's widget is shown on the web, on Android and on the TV; on the TV it is displayed, not operated. Plugins · Security model and plugin sandbox

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
How the server is put together: the hexagonal layering under internal/, the bounded contexts, the events that connect them, and the static guards that keep the code on those rails. The code lives in internal/domain, internal/app, internal/adapters/{driving,driven} and is wired in cmd/evey/wire*.go; the layout is decided by ADR-0001, the repository split by ADR-0009 and the event bus by ADR-0010. For building and running, read DEV.md; for which files to touch for a given change, read the Codebase map.

Backend is Go; the web, mobile and TV clients are a TypeScript/React monorepo under frontend/ (React Native / Expo for mobile and TV).

docs.title: Layering
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    driving[Driving adapters<br/>internal/adapters/driving<br/>grpcapi, http, pluginhost]
    app[Application services<br/>internal/app/context]
    domain[Domain<br/>internal/domain/context<br/>models, value objects, ports]
    driven[Driven adapters<br/>internal/adapters/driven<br/>postgres, ffmpeg, mkvgo, ...]
    driving --> app --> domain
    driven -. implement the ports .-> domain
Directory Holds Rule internal/domain/<context>/ models, value objects and the ports (interfaces) no framework import, no import of another context internal/app/<context>/ application services that orchestrate the ports IO goes through a port; dlna (SSDP / UPnP AVTransport) and loadtest (its own HTTP client) are the two deliberate exceptions that reach the network directly internal/adapters/driven/ outbound adapters implementing the ports: postgres, meilisearch, ffmpeg, mkvgo, filesystem, prober, opensubtitles, email, webpush, webhooksender, pluginrunner, metadata, introproviders, search three more satisfy an app-layer interface rather than a domain port: itunes and musicbrainz (app/music.AlbumArtFetcher), ociregistry (app/updatecheck) internal/adapters/driving/ inbound adapters: grpcapi (+ grpc-gateway HTTP), http (static, auth middleware, SSE, HLS, plugin iframe assets), pluginhost (gRPC server on a Unix socket, authenticated by peer credentials, the host API sandboxed plugins call back into) internal/pkg/ the shared technical kernel: auth, logger, eventbus, i18n, metrics, tracing, ratelimit, procfork, ssrf, cache, ... internal/config/ server configuration gen/ generated proto code

Dependency rule: adapters -> app -> domain. The domain never imports the app or the adapters. Composition is hand-written (not google/wire) in cmd/evey/wire.go and its siblings wire_infra.go, wire_services.go, wire_adapters.go, wire_events.go, wire_helpers.go. Tests bypass the adapters by injecting fakes that implement the same domain ports: 20 of the 21 domain packages ship a fakes/ subpackage.

docs.title: Bounded contexts
docs.text:
Thirty-two context packages live under internal/domain/ and internal/app/: 19 exist in both layers, 2 are domain-only (ratings, shared), 11 are app-only. They collaborate partly through domain events on a shared bus; the app layer also reads a neighbouring context's domain package directly (see Relations).

Context Responsibility user accounts, auth, sessions, preferences library libraries, folders, scan jobs, media index, people, collections, a profile's favorites and thumbs (thumbs have no app service: the rating RPC stores and reads UserRatingRepository as is), trickplay, intro/credits detection media (app only) share links and stream tokens mediarequest user-submitted media requests metadata TMDB / OMDb enrichment, artwork playback streams, progress, remote control, now-playing transcoding ffmpeg jobs, HLS segments subtitle embedded + external + opensubtitles mkv MKV container ops (via mkvgo) music audio-specific playback + tagging photo photo libraries favorite (app only) per-profile favorites; the model and FavoriteRepository live in domain/library playlist user playlists, smart playlists collection (app only) admin-curated collections; its ports live in domain/library ratings (domain only) maps country classifications (CSA, FSK, MPAA, BBFC, ACB) onto one minimum-age axis feed activity feed / discover activity user activity timeline chromecast cast session lifecycle syncplay multi-device sync sessions plugin plugin registry, sandbox tokens, lifecycle notification in-app + webpush notifications webhook outbound webhooks backup DB + config backup/restore config (app only) persisted server settings, written by both the REST and the gRPC entry points dlna (app only) SSDP discovery and UPnP AVTransport control loadtest (app only) simulates HLS viewers against the server's own HTTP stack maintenance (app only) admin-triggered media maintenance: seek-index rebuild, repair journal, undo, audio integrity presence (app only) in-memory, non-persisted registry of who is connected right now qoe (app only) CMCD (CTA-5004) playback telemetry ingest and aggregation demo (app only) the public demo instance (EVEY_DEMO=1): seeds its accounts, libraries and freely licensed media through the product's own services, and resets itself updatecheck (app only) compares the running build with what the registry publishes and tells the administrator; it never updates anything shared (domain only) cross-cutting ports (EventBus, TransactionalUnit, ServerConfigRepository, ShareLinkRepository), typed ids, cursors, stream tokens

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
Emitter Events Consumed by library LibraryCreated / LibraryDeleted, LibraryScanStarted / LibraryScanCompleted, MediaItemAdded, MediaItemRemoved, TrickplayGenerated media.item.added: notification, metadata (auto-enrich), library itself (trickplay worker + intro detection), feed (genre-cache invalidation) playback PlaybackStarted / PlaybackStopped no dedicated subscriber today; only webhook's "*" catch-all receives them user UserCreated, user.password.reset_requested the first has no subscriber; the second is consumed by the email driven adapter pluginrunner plugin.error / plugin.started app/plugin for its security dashboard, notification for the administrator shared ServerConfigChanged the services that apply a setting saved in the admin panel without a restart (SMTP, timezone, CPU budget, ...)
  • Search indexing is not event-driven: library.ScanService calls the library.SearchIndex port directly.
  • There is no bridge feeding domain events into plugins: plugins reach the API with scoped JWTs (ADR-0003). The bus itself is ADR-0010.
  • shared.TransactionalUnit wraps multi-aggregate writes (ADR-0002).

No package under internal/domain imports another context's domain package, a rule enforced by internal/contractguard/domain_imports_test.go (see Architecture guards). The app layer is not bound by it: 15 app packages import a neighbouring context's domain package today.

docs.title: Typical data flow - "user plays a media"
docs.text:
1. Mobile/web client calls POST /api/v1/playback/start (grpc-gateway route).
  2. internal/adapters/driving/http runs its auth middleware (auth_middleware.go, httpAuthMiddleware), extracts session.
  3. internal/adapters/driving/grpcapi (playback_handler.go) validates proto, calls app/playback.CommandService.StartStream (command/query split, see ADR-0009).
  4. app/playback.CommandService calls domain ports: user.UserRepository, playback.SessionQueryRepo (idempotency + device cap), playback.SessionCommandRepo, then shared.EventBus.Publish(PlaybackStarted).
  5. Driven adapters execute: postgres persists the session inside a shared.TransactionalUnit.Do scope; the in-process bus (internal/pkg/eventbus) dispatches asynchronously.
  6. PlaybackStarted has no dedicated subscriber today: only the webhook "*" catch-all receives it.
  7. Response streams back through grpc-gateway as JSON; progress updates flow over SSE / gRPC streams.

What happens once the player asks for the manifest and the segments is the subject of Playback pipeline.

docs.title: Architecture guards
docs.text:
The rules above are not documentation-only. internal/contractguard/ holds 58 static tests across 30 files that fail the build when the codebase drifts from them.

The hexagonal rule itself is TestDomainContextsDoNotImportEachOther (ADR-0001), in domain_imports_test.go. It walks internal/domain and enforces exactly this: a context may import internal/domain/shared and its own package tree, nothing else from internal/domain, and never internal/app or internal/adapters. Its scope stops at internal/domain: it says nothing about the app layer.

The rest guard contracts that cross a language or a process boundary, among them:

Guard What it refuses TestNoClientReadOfAFieldTheServerNeverWrites a proto response field a client reads that no server code writes TestRegisteredHandlersGetEveryPortTheyDeclare, TestBootInstallsItsSilentWirings wiring that would otherwise fail silently TestPostgresRepositoriesBoundTheirQueries a Postgres repository query without a timeout TestProcfork_EveryForkGoesThroughCommand a subprocess fork that bypasses internal/pkg/procfork TestEverySortFieldTheAPIAcceptsHasASQLColumn, ...CanBuildACursorValue a sort field missing from the SQL column map or the cursor encoder TestEveryWebSurfaceReachingAnAdminRPCIsClassified, plus its native counterpart for mobile and TV a UI surface calling an admin-only RPC without deciding who sees it TestEveryAllowedSlotIsMountedOnWebAndMobile, TestPluginBridgeParityWebMobile a plugin UI slot or bridge message present on one client only TestImageSubtitleCodecsAgreeAcrossServerAndClients a second list of bitmap subtitle codecs on a player TestHandWrittenClientTypesMatchTheEndpointTheyCall a hand-written mobile/TV response type that drifts from its endpoint TestOnlyThePlanDecidesPlayback, TestNoCallerDerivesDownstreamOfThePlaybackPlan a playback decision taken outside the plan resolver (ADR-0030) TestRestartExitCodeAgreesWithTheEntrypoint a Go exit code and docker/entrypoint.sh disagreeing on what a restart means TestServerEmittedI18nKeysExistInCatalogue, TestI18nPlaceholdersAgreeAcrossLocales a server-emitted key missing from the catalogue, placeholders that differ between locales

Production differs from this dev topology

The install compose declares one service, evey. There is no separate evey-web container (nor the dev-only mailcatcher and Metro bundler): the binary serves the built web UI from /srv, so a reverse proxy forwards everything, UI and API, to it on :9091. Postgres and Meilisearch run inside the same container, supervised by docker/entrypoint.sh: PostgreSQL 17 with its data under /data/postgres, and the Meilisearch binary (Dockerfile, meili-download stage, pinned to 1.12.8) with its index under /data/meili. The repository's own docker-compose.yml keeps separate postgres and caddy services, described in Advanced deployments. See Install and Reverse proxy.

Goroutine notes:

  • gRPC server (grpc.Server.Serve) and HTTP server (gateway + static) each run in their own goroutines off the main wire-up in cmd/evey.
  • app/library scan jobs run on a worker pool (one goroutine per active library scan, see library.ScanService).
  • ffmpeg jobs are forked through internal/pkg/procfork by the driven ffmpeg adapter (ffmpeg.Transcoder.Start), one supervising goroutine per job draining the process stderr.
  • shared.EventBus dispatches subscribers asynchronously: each subscriber runs in its own goroutine so a slow consumer never blocks publishers. The bus opens no transaction of its own; that is the handler's job.
  • pluginrunner spawns one subprocess per plugin; iframe plugins live inside the user browser and talk back via signed tokens issued by app/plugin.

docs.title: Plugin sandbox and threat model
docs.text: What the server does to contain a plugin: the checks at install, the layers at run time, the sandbox modes, and what each still cannot stop. The code lives in internal/adapters/driven/pluginrunner (install analysis, sandbox), cmd/evey-plugin-launcher (Landlock and the kernel seccomp filter), sandbox/sandbox.c (the LD_PRELOAD filter) and internal/adapters/driving/pluginhost (the host API plugins call); the design is decided by ADR-0012, ADR-0013 and ADR-0014. If you are writing a plugin and want to know what you may declare and what will be refused, read Permissions and slots; to know which sandbox your machine gets, read Plugin sandbox setup.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
Plugins run as separate processes that talk to the server over gRPC on Unix sockets. The server trusts no plugin code by default. The risks it defends against, from the most to the least severe:

  1. Impersonation - a plugin pretends to be another plugin to use its permissions.
  2. Privilege escalation - a plugin escapes its sandbox and runs commands as the server.
  3. Filesystem access - a plugin reads or writes outside its own directory, in particular the server's secrets.
  4. Network exfiltration - a plugin sends data to a host of its choosing.
  5. Resource abuse - mining, fork bombs, memory or disk exhaustion.
  6. Supply chain - obfuscated or compiled code the analysis cannot read.
flowchart LR
    zip[Package] --> ex[ZIP extraction<br/>limits, no symlink, no setuid]
    ex --> man[Manifest<br/>permissions]
    man --> an[Static analysis<br/>CRITICAL refuses]
    an --> sig[Signature<br/>cosign policy]
    sig --> prev[Administrator preview<br/>accepts or refuses]
    prev --> run[Run time]
    subgraph run[Run time - every mode]
        fs[Filesystem<br/>own directory only]
        net[Network<br/>no IP socket, Fetch broker]
        sys[System calls<br/>seccomp denylist]
        uid[Separate user<br/>or user namespace]
        sock[Host socket<br/>SO_PEERCRED identity]
        res[Resource monitor<br/>memory, PIDs, disk, nice]
    end

docs.title: ZIP extraction
docs.text:
Before any file is written (pluginrunner/zip.go):

  • at most 5,000 entries, 100 MB per file, 500 MB uncompressed in total, and a compression ratio of 100:1 above 1 MB uncompressed (decompression bombs);
  • entries whose path leaves the archive (..) are refused;
  • symbolic links are refused;
  • setuid, setgid and sticky bits are removed.

docs.title: Manifest and permissions
docs.text:
The manifest declares the permissions a plugin requests. An unknown permission refuses the install. They are then enforced:

  • subprocess allows child processes. Without it, process creation is refused by the kernel (-deny-fork), and the LD_PRELOAD filter also refuses execve for interpreted plugins.
  • native-binary allows shipping compiled code or archives, which the analysis cannot read.
  • API permissions (api.library, api.user, api.metadata, media.read, media.write, notification.sender...) are checked on every call to the host by PluginPermissionInterceptor.

The full list is in Permissions and slots.

docs.title: Static analysis
docs.text:
Every file of the package is scanned by pluginrunner.AnalyzePlugin, after a normalisation pass that undoes common obfuscation (aliases, string concatenation, f-strings):

Category Severity Examples shell_exec CRITICAL os.system, subprocess.run, child_process.exec, PHP system()/shell_exec()/proc_open(), preg_replace /e, Ruby backticks, open('\|cmd') network WARNING / CRITICAL requests.get, fetch, reverse and bind shells filesystem WARNING / CRITICAL /etc/passwd, .ssh/, rm -rf, symlink operations obfuscation CRITICAL eval, base64 decoding, hex sequences, __builtins__, base64 -d \| bash privilege CRITICAL setuid, chmod 4777, sudo, signalling PID 1 cryptomining CRITICAL stratum+tcp, xmrig, cryptonight runtime_install CRITICAL pip install, npm install, curl ... \| sh dynamic_import CRITICAL __import__(), importlib.import_module sandbox_escape CRITICAL vm.runIn*, process.binding, new Function, __subclasses__(), __mro__ deserialization CRITICAL / WARNING pickle.loads, marshal.loads, __reduce__; WARNING: yaml.load() without a Loader native_code CRITICAL / WARNING ctypes.CDLL, ffi.Library; WARNING: Go unsafe compiled_binary WARNING, then BLOCK .so, .dll, .exe, .wasm, .jar embedded_archive WARNING, then BLOCK .zip, .tar.gz mime_mismatch treated as CRITICAL an extension that claims an image, with other content suspicious_url WARNING a non-HTTP scheme in a URL literal unvendored_deps WARNING requirements.txt or package.json without vendored modules

A CRITICAL finding or a mime_mismatch refuses the install. compiled_binary and embedded_archive refuse it unless the manifest declares native-binary.

What the analysis cannot guarantee

It works on patterns. It resolves known obfuscation classes (string concatenation into a callable over several steps, builtin lookup by name, Function.constructor escapes), each with a regression fixture in tests/fixtures/plugins/malicious/, but it cannot follow every transformation done at run time (strrev("metsys"), decoding a payload read from a file). It also matches inside comments: a # pip install foo comment triggers runtime_install. The enforcement boundary is the run-time sandbox, not the analysis: a plugin that slips a pattern past it still cannot read the server's data, call a denied system call, exceed its resource limits, or call a host method it has no permission for.

docs.title: Signature
docs.text:
A package can be signed with cosign. EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_POLICY sets what a failed verification does (pluginrunner/cosign.go):

Policy Effect off The signature is not checked. warn (default) A failure is recorded and shown to the administrator, without blocking. With no public key configured, nothing is verified. enforce A failure refuses the install or the update.

The public key is given by EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY.

docs.title: Administrator preview
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/admin/plugins/preview runs the analysis without installing. The administrator sees the requested permissions, every finding with its file, line and category, the URLs found in the code, and the SHA256 of the package; the same hash is checked when the install is applied, so the package analysed is the package installed. An update shows the difference in permissions, slots and hosts, and a new permission requires an explicit acknowledgement.

The administrator is the trust boundary for elevated permissions: Evey shows the surface, the administrator accepts or refuses.

docs.title: At run time
docs.text: Six layers hold in every sandbox mode; how the first two are enforced depends on the mode.

docs.title: Filesystem
docs.text: A plugin sees its own directory and its socket directory, and not the server's data, through a Landlock allowlist (landlock) or a bubblewrap mount whitelist (bubblewrap, strict). In basic mode on a kernel without Landlock there is no per-path confinement: the separate user and file permissions are then what protect the server's secrets.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
A plugin has no direct network access, whatever it declares: every IP socket is refused (-deny-inet in landlock and basic, a network namespace in bubblewrap and strict). A plugin with the network permission calls the host's Fetch method over its Unix socket. The host, in internal/adapters/driving/pluginhost/fetch.go:

  • checks the target against the plugin's external_fetch list (exact hosts, case-insensitive);
  • allows only http and https, and only GET and HEAD;
  • connects through an SSRF-safe client (internal/pkg/ssrf) that refuses private, reserved and link-local addresses after DNS resolution, so DNS rebinding and redirects are checked again (a redirect to a host off the list is refused);
  • adds none of the server's credentials, caps the response body at 8 MiB and the request headers at 8 KiB, and gives up after 20 s.

This closes the paths direct egress left open (IP literals such as 169.254.169.254, a plugin's own resolver). What remains: the broker controls where a call goes, not what it carries. See Known limits.

Recommended for operators

The broker moves the SSRF surface to the host. An egress rule on the evey-server container, independent of the code, adds a second wall: drop 169.254.0.0/16 and restrict the internal network to the database and search endpoints.

docs.title: System calls
docs.text:
Two seccomp filters refuse the same dangerous system calls:

  1. The kernel filter, installed by evey-plugin-launcher just before it starts the plugin (seccomp_linux.go). It is inherited by the plugin and its children and also covers compiled, static binaries. A mismatched architecture in a system call kills the process. Applied in landlock and basic.
  2. The LD_PRELOAD filter, sandbox/sandbox.c, loaded into interpreted plugins that do not declare subprocess. It also refuses execve/execveat, and marks the plugin non-dumpable. Applied in landlock, basic and strict. If the library is missing, such a plugin is refused start (plugin.error).

Refused system calls:

Category System calls Debugging ptrace, process_vm_readv, process_vm_writev Signals tgkill, rt_sigqueueinfo, rt_tgsigqueueinfo towards any process but the plugin itself (both filters); kill likewise in the kernel filter, towards any target in the LD_PRELOAD filter; tkill in the kernel filter (the LD_PRELOAD filter allows it towards the plugin itself); pidfd_send_signal, pidfd_getfd (steals a file descriptor). A runtime re-raising a signal or preempting its own threads keeps working. On Landlock ABI 6+, a plugin also cannot signal a process outside its sandbox Mounts mount, umount2, pivot_root, chroot Namespaces unshare, setns, and clone carrying a CLONE_NEW* flag (unshare by another name), for every plugin Kernel modules init_module, finit_module, delete_module BPF, perf bpf, perf_event_open Hardware I/O ioperm, iopl (x86-64 only, where they exist) Swap swapon, swapoff System control syslog, reboot, settimeofday, clock_settime, clock_adjtime, adjtimex Kexec kexec_load, kexec_file_load Kernel exploit primitives io_uring_setup, io_uring_enter, io_uring_register, userfaultfd Identity setuid, setgid, setreuid, setregid, setresuid, setresgid, capset Keyring add_key, request_key, keyctl

For a plugin without subprocess, the kernel also refuses process creation (fork, vfork, clone without CLONE_THREAD; clone3 answers ENOSYS so the C library falls back to clone); threads keep working.

This is a denylist: open, read, write, mmap, Unix socket and connect stay allowed. Paths are confined by the filesystem layer, not by seccomp. In bubblewrap the launcher is not used: a static binary gets no seccomp filter there, and is contained by the namespaces and the mount whitelist.

docs.title: A separate user
docs.text:
A plugin can run as user 1001 (evey-plugin), distinct from the server (1000), so the server's secrets are unreadable to it by file permissions alone. EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION controls it:

Value When the switch happens auto (default) only when the sandbox resolves to basic, the one case where file permissions are the only wall around the secrets on always, as an extra layer off never

The switch is made by the launcher, which holds cap_setuid; the server itself runs without privileges or capabilities. The launcher refuses any target below 1000. If it cannot switch, a plugin in basic is refused (the user is the only wall there), while in landlock it runs as the server's user with a warning. In bubblewrap and strict, the user namespace plays this role.

When active, the signing key (0600) and the backups (0700 directory, 0600 files) are owner-only at run time, which holds even on a bind-mounted /data. All plugins share user 1001: they are isolated from each other by the filesystem layer, not by the user.

docs.title: Host socket authentication
docs.text: Each plugin has its own socket, /tmp/evey/plugins/<plugin_id>/host.sock, served by its own gRPC server. On every call, the server reads the caller's PID from the kernel (SO_PEERCRED, which user space cannot forge) and compares it with the PID recorded when the plugin started. The plugin's identity comes from the socket, never from a header. A plugin therefore cannot impersonate another, call another plugin's socket, or route calls through a child process. A PID mismatch is logged as a warning.

docs.title: Resource limits
docs.text:
A monitor in user space (cgroups are unavailable in an unprivileged container) reads /proc/<pid> every 2 seconds and stops a plugin that exceeds a limit (ADR-0013):

Limit Default Checked memory (RSS) 256 MiB every sweep processes and threads 64 every sweep disk used by its directory 100 MiB every 15th sweep, about 30 s CPU priority nice 10, applied at start -

The same sweep flags a plugin that keeps a CPU pegged above 90% for about 30 s, and stops a plugin granted hardware.gpu that keeps a graphics engine pegged the same way. The limits are set per plugin in Admin → Plugins → Resource limits; the environment variables EVEY_PLUGINS_MEMORY_MB, EVEY_PLUGINS_PIDS_MAX, EVEY_PLUGINS_DISK_MAX_MB and EVEY_PLUGINS_CPU_NICE set the boot defaults.

docs.title: Interface isolation
docs.text: A plugin's interface runs in an <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts">, without same-origin access, forms or popups, under a Content-Security-Policy that allows connections only to its external_fetch hosts. The bridge (frontend/packages/client/src/plugins/hostProtocol.ts) limits what it can ask of the page: toast at most 3 per second, 200 characters, no HTML; navigate accepts only /home, /library, /media, /player, /settings and /search; resize between 50 px (60 on mobile and TV) and 800 px. Slots are checked at install and again at render.

docs.title: Server hardening
docs.text: At startup the server marks itself non-dumpable (PR_SET_DUMPABLE=0, hardening_linux.go): a process running as the same user cannot read its memory or environment through /proc, which protects the signing key in memory and the database and search passwords, even on a kernel without Landlock.

docs.title: Crash notification
docs.text: The runner publishes a plugin.error event when the sandbox library is missing for a plugin that needs it, or when a plugin exits with an error. The notification service forwards it to the administrator through the configured channels, and the Security Dashboard records it.

docs.title: Sandbox modes
docs.text:
The mode selects how the filesystem and the network are confined. EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE sets the initial value (default auto); it can be changed in Admin → Plugins → Resource limits → Sandbox mode. The runner applies it in applySandbox. In every mode: no direct IP egress, the resource monitor, and the host socket authentication.

Layer landlock basic bubblewrap strict Filesystem Landlock allowlist none without Landlock (file permissions only) mount whitelist mount whitelist Network -restrict-net + -deny-inet -deny-inet network namespace network namespace Kernel seccomp (static binaries too) yes yes no no LD_PRELOAD seccomp (interpreted plugins without subprocess) yes yes no yes Separate user with on yes (auto) user namespace user namespace Resource limits yes yes yes yes

docs.title: auto (default)
docs.text:
Resolves, once at the first plugin start, to the strongest mode the host supports: landlock when the kernel enforces Landlock and the evey-plugin-launcher binary is found (next to the server binary, on $PATH, or at EVEY_PLUGIN_LAUNCHER); otherwise bubblewrap when a test sandbox actually builds (ProbeSandbox), which in practice means bare metal or a privileged container; otherwise basic. Landlock comes first because it needs no privilege and runs under Docker's default security profile. The resolved mode is logged, and shown on the Host sandbox line of Admin → Plugins → Security Dashboard.

Deployment What auto gives Docker on a recent kernel landlock: per-path confinement, no direct egress, dangerous system calls refused including static binaries. The normal case. Docker on an old kernel without Landlock, e.g. an old NAS basic: secrets protected and network cut, but world-readable files visible. See Plugin sandbox setup. Bare metal bubblewrap: the strongest filesystem and process isolation, without a seccomp filter for static binaries.

docs.title: landlock
docs.text:
• Filesystem: a Landlock allowlist applied by the launcher. System directories (/usr, /lib, /lib64, /bin, /sbin, /etc, /app) read-only; of /dev, only null, zero, full, random and urandom, so graphics card nodes and the server's terminal stay out of reach; the plugin's directory and socket directory read-write; everything else, including /data and other plugins, denied. A plugin granted hardware.gpu gets its render node as the one exception.
  • Network: -restrict-net and -deny-inet; egress only through Fetch.
  • System calls: the kernel filter and the LD_PRELOAD filter.
  • Requires: a kernel 5.13 or newer with Landlock in the active LSM list, and the launcher (both are the case on the official image with a recent host). An explicit landlock refuses to start a plugin it cannot confine.

docs.title: bubblewrap
docs.text:
• Filesystem and processes: six unshared namespaces (user, pid, uts, ipc, cgroup, net) and a mount whitelist; nothing else exists inside (buildBwrapCmd in pluginrunner/runner_bwrap.go).
Path Access /usr, /bin, /sbin, /lib, /lib64 read-only /etc/ssl, /etc/ca-certificates, /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/nsswitch.conf, /etc/{alpine,os}-release read-only (never /etc as a whole: no passwd, shadow, ssh) the plugin's directory, its socket directory read-write /proc its own mount /dev a minimal synthetic set (null, zero, random, urandom, tty, pts) /tmp an empty tmpfs

/data, /var, /home, /root, /run and other plugins' directories do not exist inside. A canary plugin (tests/fixtures/plugins/canary-sandbox-runtime/) checks this layout against a running stack. - Network: the network namespace, for every plugin. - System calls: no seccomp filter; the namespaces provide the isolation. - Requires: the bwrap binary and the mount/unshare system calls. In Docker that needs a relaxed security profile, so this is effectively a bare-metal mode.

docs.title: strict
docs.text: bubblewrap plus the LD_PRELOAD filter (interpreted plugins only).

docs.title: basic
docs.text: The last resort of auto: the separate user, the kernel filter, the LD_PRELOAD filter, -deny-inet, and Landlock if the kernel has it. On a kernel without Landlock there is no per-path confinement: a plugin can read non-sensitive world-readable files and see the process list. The server's secrets stay protected by the separate user and PR_SET_DUMPABLE, the network is cut, and dangerous system calls are refused, compiled binaries included.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Variable Default Effect EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE auto auto, landlock, bubblewrap, strict or basic. Also editable in Admin → Plugins. EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION auto auto, on or off. Incompatible with no_new_privs on the container. EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_POLICY warn off, warn or enforce. EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY none The key signatures are checked against. EVEY_PLUGINS_MEMORY_MB, EVEY_PLUGINS_PIDS_MAX, EVEY_PLUGINS_DISK_MAX_MB, EVEY_PLUGINS_CPU_NICE 256, 64, 100, 10 Boot defaults of the resource limits; the panel overrides them per plugin.

The official image ships evey-plugin-launcher (Landlock and the kernel filter) and bubblewrap. bubblewrap also needs unprivileged user namespaces on the host. Which setup fits which machine, in plain terms: Plugin sandbox setup.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text: Limit Impact What limits it today No per-path confinement in basic on a kernel without Landlock A plugin can read non-sensitive world-readable files and other plugins' directories Secrets protected by the separate user and PR_SET_DUMPABLE; auto prefers Landlock or bubblewrap All plugins share user 1001 A plugin can signal its siblings (signalling the server is refused) PR_SET_DUMPABLE blocks reading other processes through /proc; Landlock and bubblewrap isolate plugin directories Seccomp is a denylist File and Unix socket calls stay allowed Paths are confined by Landlock or bubblewrap; IP sockets are refused The broker moves the SSRF surface to the host A flaw in the broker's validation could reach an internal address Allowlist and SSRF-safe client in Go; an egress rule on the container as an independent layer The broker controls where a call goes, not what it carries Data can leave towards a host on the plugin's list Allow only hosts you trust with that data The analysis works on patterns Deliberate obfuscation can hide code Administrator preview; the sandbox, not the analysis, is the boundary LD_PRELOAD only covers dynamic, interpreted plugins A static binary in basic without the launcher escapes it The official image always ships the launcher, whose kernel filter covers static binaries

docs.title: Network exposure (outside the plugin threat model)
docs.text:
Two invariants govern who can reach the server at all:

  • Only the HTTP port is meant to be published. The gRPC port (EVEY_SERVER_PORT, default 9090) is an internal transport whose only client is the HTTP gateway in the same process; the HTTP API is that port plus one. gRPC binds to loopback by default (EVEY_GRPC_BIND=127.0.0.1) because the remote-access gate is HTTP middleware and does not cover it. Widening the bind logs a warning; firewalling it is then the operator's job.
  • The remote-access gate decides from the one client address validated at the trusted proxy boundary, never from a request header. A client cannot claim 127.0.0.1 through X-Forwarded-For, and a request that never crossed that boundary counts as remote. This is a deployment control, not authentication.

See Remote access and HTTPS and the Configuration reference.

docs.title: What the logs may contain
docs.text: The server log feeds Logs & Debug, bug reports and backups, so credentials are scrubbed when a line is written (internal/pkg/logger/redact.go): an attribute whose key names a secret (authorization, token, api_key, password, pin, secret...) is replaced whole, and any string carrying a bearer token, a JWT or a secret=value pair is scrubbed. The log routes apply the same rule to older lines on the way out. For code: never log a non-secret value under a secret key name (it will be masked), and add a new kind of credential to that list before it is ever logged.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text: Report privately, never in a public issue: security@eveyproject.org, the address of the repository's security policy. It covers plugin authentication, permissions and sandbox escapes like anything else. Do not test against Evey instances that are not yours.

docs.title: Backups and updates
docs.text: A scheduled backup of the database, kept for as long as you choose, and an update that is a docker compose pull away. This page is for the administrator: what a backup holds and what it does not, how to restore one, and how to update or go back without losing data.

docs.title: What a backup contains
docs.text:
A backup is a copy of the database: accounts, profiles, libraries and their catalogue, watch history and resume points, collections, playlists and favourites, settings, plugin records, webhooks, API keys, notifications and audit logs. It is a .tar.gz holding the SQL dump and a manifest with the dump's SHA256 and the schema version.

It does not contain:

  • your media files;
  • the transcoding cache (regenerated on demand);
  • the search index (rebuilt from the database);
  • the keys kept in ./evey-data: jwt.key, which signs sessions, and the keys folder (database password, search key);
  • the installed plugin files.

A database backup therefore restores Evey's state on the same installation. To be able to rebuild a machine, keep a copy of the whole ./evey-data folder as well: the database backups are inside it, in ./evey-data/backups.

docs.title: Schedule backups
docs.text:
Admin → Database Backup → Schedule: a Cron expression (for example 0 3 * * *, every day at 3 AM) and a Retention (days). Backups older than the retention are deleted after each scheduled run. Run now makes one immediately, as does Create Backup at the top of the page.

A backup every day at 3 AM, kept 30 days.

The server also dumps the database on its own before applying a migration during an update, whatever the schedule (see Updating Evey).

docs.title: Restore a backup
docs.text:
Admin → Database Backup lists the backups and restores one, or restores from a file you upload (Restore from File). Restoring replaces the current database.

Same schema only

The server checks the checksum and the schema version first, and refuses a backup taken by a version with a different schema instead of loading it. To go back to an older version with its data, see Going back.

When the server does not start any more, the command line restores the dumps taken before a migration (pre-migration-*.sql.gz), not the .tar.gz backups of this panel: see Recovery.

docs.title: Updating Evey
docs.text:
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f evey

That is the whole update. When the new version needs to change the database, it first writes a dump to ./evey-data/backups/pre-migration-*.sql.gz (the three most recent are kept), then applies the migrations while starting; a large catalogue can take a few minutes, and the container reports healthy once it serves again. Evey asks the registry every hour whether a newer image is published and says so in the admin panel; it never updates itself.

Pin what you run. During the beta there is no numbered release and no latest tag; the branch tag beta-0.0.1 moves with every change. For a server you rely on, put an immutable sha-<commit> tag on the image: line, so that two pulls a day apart run the same code. Once releases exist, latest will follow the most recent stable one, and a release tag (0.2.0) will pin it.

Which version is running. docker exec evey-server evey version prints the version and the commit of the running binary.

docs.title: Going back
docs.text:
Put the previous tag on the image: line and run docker compose up -d. If the newer version had migrated the database, restore its pre-migration dump first: docker exec evey-server evey admin rollback prints the exact steps with the dump's path.

Image tags, runtime variants and GPU flavours are described in Advanced deployments.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text: Where each setting of an Evey server lives, which value wins when a setting exists both in the admin panel and in the environment, and what a restart is needed for. The variables themselves are listed by topic in the ten pages linked below; this page is for the administrator who edits the compose file or wonders why a variable seems ignored.

docs.title: Two places, one rule
docs.text:
What must exist before the server starts - secrets, storage paths, the public address, reverse-proxy facts - goes in the compose file as environment variables. What an administrator tunes afterwards - languages, transcoding limits, hardware acceleration, schedules, plugin limits - lives in the admin panel, is stored in the database, survives a container update and mostly applies without a restart.

For a setting that exists in both places, the precedence is always the same:

  1. The value saved in the panel wins. At every start the server reads the environment first, then replaces each field with the value stored in the database when one exists. A variable never overrides a saved value.
  2. The variable applies while nothing is saved. The panel shows it as the current default; Reset to default removes the saved value, and the variable applies again from the next start.
  3. The built-in default applies when neither is set.

Secrets are the exception: the panel never shows a password or a key it stored, and a variable such as EVEY_TMDB_API_KEY is copied into the database on first use so the panel can display that a custom key is in use.

docs.title: What needs a restart
docs.text:
• A change to an environment variable always needs the container recreated (docker compose up -d): the process reads its environment once.
  • A change in the panel applies live for most settings (server name, log level, rate limits, hardware acceleration, SMTP, single sign-on, remote access, plugin limits, retention windows at the next daily sweep).
  • The panel marks the settings that are read at startup with applies on restart: the library watcher and scan interval, the transcode cache budget, the Advanced limits card of Transcoding, the intro providers, and every Config entries row. Saving stores the choice, restarting applies it.

Each table in the topic pages has a Panel column: the path to the field (starting at Admin) and whether it applies live or at restart, or none when the variable has no panel equivalent.

Page Covers Server and network Public address, ports, reverse proxy, remote access, request limits, container user Database and search Embedded or external Postgres and Meilisearch Accounts and sign-in Session lifetimes, signing key, single sign-on Libraries and metadata Scanning, metadata keys, intro detection Transcoding and hardware Graphics card, capacity, quality limits, cache, calibration clip Playback delivery and downloads Stream packaging switches, prepared downloads, player skip buttons Background work Background passes and their pacing Plugins and sandbox Sandbox mode, separate user, resource limits, signatures E-mail and notifications SMTP, browser push keys Backups, logs and monitoring Backups, log, history retention, metrics and tracing

docs.title: How values are read
docs.text:
• Booleans accept 1, t, true, 0, f, false. Durations need a unit: 30s, 5m, 2h (a bare 30 is ignored). Lists are comma-separated.
  • A value the server cannot parse is ignored with a warning in the log (environment variable ignored, value could not be parsed) and the default applies. Check the first lines of the log after editing the compose file.
  • EVEY_DB_PASSWORD and MEILI_MASTER_KEY can also come from a file named by the same variable with a _FILE suffix; an explicit value wins over the file.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
The embedded Postgres and Meilisearch generate their secrets on the first start, in ./evey-data/keys (postgres.password, meili.key, mode 0600). The server reads them through EVEY_DB_PASSWORD_FILE and MEILI_MASTER_KEY_FILE, set in the image, which is also why evey admin commands need no password. Set EVEY_DB_PASSWORD or MEILI_MASTER_KEY only for an external database or search engine.

A TMDB key is built in. EVEY_TMDB_API_KEY seeds your own; the key set in Admin → Server Config → API Keys wins over it.

docs.title: Variables you do not need
docs.text:
Lines often carried over from older setups, and why they change nothing:

Line Why it is unnecessary EVEY_LOG_DIR, EVEY_TRANSCODING_CACHE_DIR, EVEY_TRICKPLAY_CACHE_DIR The image already sets these to /data/logs, /cache/transcode, /data/trickplay. Repeating them changes nothing. EVEY_FORWARDED_PROTO Deprecated - derived from the scheme of EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL. Setting it only logs a deprecation warning. EVEY_KEYFRAME_BACKFILL=on Anything other than off enables it, including absent. LIBVA_DRIVER_NAME libva picks the driver from the GPU's PCI id. Force it only if your card needs a driver libva does not choose (verify with docker exec evey-server vainfo). EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE auto picks the strongest confinement your host supports. Set it explicitly only when you want a fail-closed guarantee - landlock refuses to run a plugin it cannot confine, where auto degrades with a warning. a group_add for /dev/dri/card0 Evey only ever opens renderD128. Check with ls -ln /dev/dri and add that group alone.

docs.title: File ownership (PUID and PGID)
docs.text:
Default: automatic. When PUID/PGID are not set, the entrypoint looks at the owner of your /media* mounts at startup and runs the server as that user, so the features that write into your library (the seek-index repair rebuilds files in place) work out of the box - no chown, no configuration. The startup log tells you what was picked:

evey: media mounts owned by 1026:100 (detected on /media) - running the
server as that user so write features (seek-index repair) work out of the box

Media mounts owned by different users are handled best-effort: the server adopts the user owning the most mounts and joins the other mounts' groups as supplementary groups, so repairs on those mounts work when their files are group-writable (the startup warning lists which mounts may still refuse writes). Auto-detection only steps aside entirely (falls back to 1000:1000 with a warning) when every media mount is owned by root or by the reserved uid 1001 - chown your media to a regular user, or set PUID/PGID explicitly:

.env
PUID=1026   # run the server as this user id  (host: `id -u <media-owner>`)
PGID=100    # ...and this group id

Explicit values always win over detection.

How it works: the container starts as root just long enough to re-map its internal user (and re-own Evey's own state directories /data, /cache - never your media mounts), then drops privileges. Supplementary groups granted via compose group_add: (e.g. your host's render group for /dev/dri hardware transcoding) are preserved across the drop. The server process itself never runs as root.

Zero-root alternative: if even that transient root is unacceptable to you, set user: "UID:GID" on the service in your compose file instead. The entrypoint detects the non-root start and skips the re-map (including the media-owner detection) - you then own keeping ./evey-data writable by that UID yourself.

Note

PUID=1001 is refused: it is the internal evey-plugin user, kept distinct so plugins can never share the server's identity. Media is mounted read-write by default so repairs work natively; append :ro to the media volume if you prefer a read-only library (repairs then fail with a clear error).

docs.title: Variables the server does not read
docs.text:
Some variables appear in compose files without being read by the server:

  • EVEY_HTTP_PORT, EVEY_DOMAIN, MEDIA_DIR: used by the repository's own docker-compose.yml (published port, the bundled Caddy's domain, the media path), not by Evey. EVEY_VERSION is the image tag there; the server only shows it on /healthz when its binary carries no version.
  • EVEY_WEB_DIR (/srv, where the web interface files are), and EVEY_DB_PASSWORD_FILE, MEILI_MASTER_KEY_FILE, EVEY_IMAGE_REPO, EVEY_IMAGE_RUNTIMES: match the image's layout. Changing them is not supported.
  • EVEY_SUPERVISED, EVEY_COMPANION_PIDS, EVEY_RESTART_EXIT_CODE, EVEY_LAUNCHER_BIN, EVEY_PLUGIN_LAUNCHER: set by the entrypoint and the plugin launcher for their own use.
  • EVEY_BANNER=off only hides the start-up banner in the log; NO_COLOR removes its colours.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Where to start when you want to work on Evey's code, and what a pull request is expected to pass. The documents written for contributors live with the code, on GitHub, rather than on this site; this page points at them.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: You want to Read Build and run Evey from source DEV.md Know the rules of a contribution: branches, commits, tests, the licence agreement CONTRIBUTING.md Find your way in the code in half an hour Codebase map Understand the layering and the bounded contexts Architecture Follow the conventions the code already uses Code conventions Work on the interface Frontend design system Know why a structural choice was made Architecture decisions Cut a release Release runbook

docs.title: Why a decision record, and where
docs.text: Every structural choice - the hexagonal layout, how plugin tokens are scoped, why the install is a single compose file, how one playback plan decides for every client - has an architecture decision record: the context, the options that were weighed, what was chosen and what it costs. They are kept in the repository, next to the code they explain, and are the place to start before proposing to change one of those choices.

docs.title: Before you open a pull request
docs.text:
1. Run make pre-push: it is the gate, and runs the CI's checks locally in this order: vet, vulnerability scan, build, unit tests with -race, frontend (typecheck, lint, unit tests), security scan, lint, architecture guards, commit hygiene, secret scan, proto breaking-change check, a build from a clean checkout, the repository and transcoding integration gates, and the TV audit.
  2. Add tests for new behaviour and for every bug fix.
  3. For an external contribution, accept the contributor licence agreement once: Evey is AGPL-3.0-or-later and is also offered under a commercial licence. You keep the copyright on your work.

The gate does not build the Docker image or the Android apps

After touching the Dockerfile or Kotlin code, build them yourself (docker build --target runtime, the Gradle release task) before pushing.

Security issues are not reported in public: write to security@eveyproject.org (see SECURITY.md).

docs.title: Without a container
docs.text: How to run Evey directly on a host (systemd, an init script, or by hand) instead of the Docker image. The image is the recommended path: it ships the plugin sandbox, the hardening and the plugin runtimes already wired. Going bare metal means reproducing that posture yourself: the right binaries side by side, a dedicated non-root user, the sandbox backend your kernel supports, and owner-only secret directories. This page walks through it in order.

docs.title: Build and install the binaries
docs.text:
Build the two Go binaries and install them in the same directory: the plugin runner looks for the launcher in $EVEY_PLUGIN_LAUNCHER first, then next to its own executable, then on $PATH.

# from the repository root
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags="-s -w -X main.version=$(git describe --tags --always) -X main.commit=$(git rev-parse HEAD)" -o evey ./cmd/evey
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o evey-plugin-launcher ./cmd/evey-plugin-launcher
sudo install -m 0755 evey evey-plugin-launcher /opt/evey/

# optional: shell completion and the manual page, both printed by the binary
/opt/evey/evey completion bash | sudo tee /etc/bash_completion.d/evey >/dev/null
/opt/evey/evey man | sudo tee /usr/local/share/man/man1/evey.1 >/dev/null

evey version prints the version, commit and build date without any configuration.

docs.title: The seccomp shim
docs.text:
Build libevey-sandbox.so (one C file, needs a C compiler) and install it at the path the runner expects, /app/libevey-sandbox.so:

gcc -shared -fPIC -nostartfiles -o libevey-sandbox.so sandbox/sandbox.c
sudo install -D -m 0644 libevey-sandbox.so /app/libevey-sandbox.so

The path is fixed in the runner. Without the file, plugins refuse to start (fail closed) unless the server runs in dev mode. The shim adds a seccomp denylist for dynamically linked plugins, on top of Landlock or bubblewrap. The image keeps it under /app with the SDK; a symlink works too.

docs.title: Runtimes and services
docs.text:
Install whatever your plugins' entrypoint: invokes. The runner recognises python3, python, node, php, ruby, perl, lua, bash and sh; python3 covers most community plugins. Then the services the server talks to:

Dependency Why ffmpeg and ffprobe transcoding, probing; the image also bundles VAAPI drivers and fpcalc (chromaprint) for intro detection PostgreSQL (server plus a database) and pg_dump the database; pg_dump writes the automatic pre-migration dump Meilisearch the search index; without it search falls back to SQL bwrap (bubblewrap) only for the bubblewrap sandbox backend setcap (libcap) to grant the launcher its file capability

The embedded database and search engine are a feature of the image's entrypoint, not of the binary: on bare metal you run both yourself and point EVEY_DB_HOST and EVEY_MEILI_URL at them.

docs.title: Run as a dedicated non-root user
docs.text:
Never run the server as root. Create a group and two unprivileged users, as the image does:

sudo groupadd --gid 1000 evey
sudo useradd --system --uid 1000 --gid evey --shell /usr/sbin/nologin evey
sudo useradd --system --uid 1001 --gid evey --shell /usr/sbin/nologin evey-plugin
  • evey (UID 1000) runs the server.
  • evey-plugin (UID 1001) is the user plugins are dropped to when uid separation is active, so a compromised plugin lands as a different unprivileged user that cannot read the server's secrets by plain file permissions.

Warning

The group id matters: the launcher drops a plugin to UID 1001 and to the server's own group, and refuses any uid or gid below 1000. A group created by useradd --system alone gets a system id below 1000, and plugins in basic mode are then refused.

The server marks itself non-dumpable at startup (PR_SET_DUMPABLE=0), so a co-resident plugin cannot read /proc/<server-pid>/{mem,environ}.

docs.title: Pick the sandbox backend for your kernel
docs.text: Set EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE. auto (the default) resolves in the order landlock, bubblewrap, basic and picks the strongest the host supports. Set a mode explicitly when you want fail-closed behaviour.

docs.title: Landlock (recommended)
docs.text:
A per-path filesystem allowlist (a plugin sees its own directory and the socket directory, never your data or secrets) plus a Landlock v4 TCP egress filter. It needs no privilege, no mount and no namespace: the launcher applies it to itself, then executes the plugin.

Landlock must be compiled in and in the active LSM list. The runner probes landlock_create_ruleset; the probe fails when the syscall is absent (kernel older than 5.13) or when Landlock is not in the active list. Check:

uname -r                              # want 5.13 or newer
cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm          # must include "landlock"

If landlock is missing from that list, add it on the kernel command line and reboot (keep the existing entries, the list varies per distribution):

# e.g. in GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX:
lsm=lockdown,capability,yama,apparmor,bpf,landlock

Then either keep auto or pin it:

EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=landlock    # fail closed: a plugin is refused when Landlock cannot be enforced

landlock passes -require-landlock to the launcher, which exits non-zero rather than run a plugin unconfined.

docs.title: bubblewrap
docs.text:
When Landlock is not available, install bwrap. It puts each plugin in user, pid, uts, ipc and network namespaces with a mount allowlist. It needs unprivileged user namespaces and the mount syscall, true on most bare-metal Linux but blocked inside an unprivileged container, which is why Landlock is the container default. auto only selects bubblewrap when Landlock is absent and a throwaway bwrap probe succeeds.

EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=bubblewrap  # namespaces
EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=strict      # namespaces plus the seccomp shim

Check that the host permits the namespace and mount setup:

bwrap --unshare-user --unshare-net --ro-bind / / /bin/true && echo "bwrap OK"

docs.title: basic (last resort)
docs.text:
EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=basic is a uid drop plus the seccomp shim; the launcher, when present, still installs its kernel seccomp denylist and best-effort Landlock. There is no per-path filesystem confinement: a plugin runs at UID 1001 with seccomp only. Use it on old or locked-down kernels where neither Landlock nor bubblewrap works, and rely on the uid separation below to protect the secrets.

A plugin granted the subprocess permission requires the launcher even in basic mode: the shim does not survive an exec of a child process, only the launcher's kernel seccomp does. Without the launcher such a plugin refuses to start rather than run unconfined.

docs.title: Keep secrets out of a plugin's reach
docs.text:
Uid separation runs each plugin under evey-plugin (UID 1001), distinct from the server (UID 1000), so a plugin cannot read jwt.key, the backups or the logs by plain file permissions. It matters in basic mode; under Landlock or bubblewrap the filesystem is already walled off, so it is redundant there.

EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION:

Value Behaviour auto (default) on only when the sandbox resolves to basic on always, as an extra independent layer off never

The drop is done by the launcher, not the server. The server stays non-root with no capability; the launcher carries one file capability and switches to UID 1001 just before executing the plugin:

sudo setcap cap_setuid+ep /opt/evey/evey-plugin-launcher

The launcher refuses any target uid or gid below 1000. When it cannot drop (capability missing, no_new_privs set), a plugin in basic mode is refused, since the uid is its only wall there; under Landlock it logs a warning and runs at the server's uid.

Warning

Uid separation is incompatible with no_new_privs. If the server runs under systemd NoNewPrivileges=yes, the file capability is ignored on exec: plugins are refused in basic mode, and under Landlock uid separation degrades to same-uid. Pick one.

If the server runs as root instead (not recommended), it drops plugins to 1001 directly and the capability is not needed. The plain-language picture per scenario is in Plugin sandbox setup.

docs.title: Secret file permissions
docs.text:
Mirror the image: secret-bearing directories are owner-only, so a plugin dropped to UID 1001 cannot read them even without Landlock.

sudo chown -R evey:evey /var/lib/evey
# the server owns plugins/ (it extracts installs there); group evey,
# which evey-plugin belongs to, only reads and executes the installed files:
sudo chmod 750 /var/lib/evey/plugins
# owner-only on the secret directories:
sudo chmod 700 /var/lib/evey/keys /var/lib/evey/logs /var/lib/evey/backups
# the JWT signing key itself (generated 0600 on first boot):
sudo chmod 600 /var/lib/evey/jwt.key

Adjust the paths to wherever you point the EVEY_*_DIR variables and EVEY_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH.

docs.title: Configure the environment
docs.text:
All configuration is EVEY_* environment variables; Configuration has the full table. Points specific to a bare-metal run:

  • Point EVEY_DB_HOST and EVEY_MEILI_URL at your PostgreSQL and Meilisearch. EVEY_DB_PASSWORD must not be the default evey.
  • The Go defaults for paths were chosen for the container: set EVEY_LOG_DIR (defaults to the relative logs), EVEY_BACKUP_DIR (/data/backups), EVEY_TRANSCODING_CACHE_DIR (/data/transcode), EVEY_TRICKPLAY_CACHE_DIR (/cache/trickplay) and EVEY_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH (/data/jwt.key) to your own directories.
  • The server serves plain HTTP: put a reverse proxy in front for TLS, with an https:// External URL and the proxy in Trusted proxies (Admin -> Remote Access; EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL and EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES are the fallbacks). See Reverse proxy.
  • The server opens two ports, and only one may be exposed. EVEY_SERVER_PORT (default 9090) is the native gRPC listener; the HTTP API your clients and reverse proxy talk to is that port plus one (9091). The remote-access gate, which decides whether clients outside your LAN may connect, is wired into the HTTP chain and does not cover the gRPC listener, which therefore binds to loopback only by default (EVEY_GRPC_BIND=127.0.0.1). If you have a reason to publish it, set EVEY_GRPC_BIND=0.0.0.0; the server warns at boot that the gate does not apply to it, and firewalling it is then on you.
  • Migrations run at startup; there is no separate migrate step.
  • The plugin resource caps (EVEY_PLUGINS_MEMORY_MB, _PIDS_MAX, _DISK_MAX_MB, _CPU_NICE) and the sandbox mode are editable at runtime from Admin -> Plugins -> Resource limits; the environment values are the initial defaults.
  • The admin panel's server restart relies on the image's supervisor and reports itself unavailable in a bare run: restart the service yourself.

docs.title: Verify the sandbox
docs.text:
The server logs the backend it resolved. After the first plugin starts, look for:

  • once, for auto: plugin sandbox auto-detection complete selected_mode=landlock (or bubblewrap, basic);
  • at every plugin start: plugin sandbox applied sandbox_mode=landlock plugin_id=...;
  • the warning you do not want when you expected Landlock: plugin sandbox auto-detection fell back to basic mode: no per-path filesystem isolation available ..., meaning neither Landlock nor a working bwrap was found. Re-check the backend section above.

Confirm the kernel side independently:

cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm              # lists "landlock"
grep Seccomp: /proc/<plugin-pid>/status   # 2 = a seccomp filter is active on the plugin

A Seccomp: 2 line on a live plugin process confirms the kernel filter is installed. With EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=landlock and Landlock not enforced, the plugin refuses to start: that is the fail-closed contract working.

For backups, updates and the recovery commands, the container pages apply as they are: Backups and updates, Recovery and the command line describe the same evey admin binary.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
Seven constraints the code follows, each with the pages and decision records where it shows. Read this page to understand why Evey behaves as it does before reading how it is built (Architecture) or why a structural choice was made (decision records). When two principles conflict, the earlier one in this list wins.

Principle Where it shows Decided by 1. Access is refused when it cannot be checked parental control, plugin install, remote access ADR-0026 2. Third-party code is contained, not trusted plugin sandbox ADR-0012, ADR-0014 3. The original is delivered whenever it can be playback decision ADR-0030 4. Decisions rest on what was proved, not on names casting, hardware acceleration ADR-0029 5. One playback, one decision playback plan, Stream info ADR-0030, ADR-0024 6. The server sizes itself to the machine calibration, background work - 7. Few settings, each in one place install, admin panel ADR-0028

docs.title: 1. Access is refused when it cannot be checked
docs.text:
Where a decision grants access, an error resolves to the most restrictive answer. A profile whose parental settings cannot be read gets no content; a plugin whose code cannot be analysed is not installed; remote access follows an explicit choice once one was made, and says loudly when it refuses everyone. Remote access and authentication are separate: the first is a deployment choice, the second is what protects the library.

See Users, profiles and parental control, Remote access and HTTPS, ADR-0026.

docs.title: 2. Third-party code is contained, not trusted
docs.text:
A plugin gets the permissions its manifest declares and nothing else, is analysed before installation, runs in a sandbox with no direct network access, and holds a token that is denied by default. What the sandbox still cannot prevent is written down rather than implied.

See Plugin sandbox and threat model, ADR-0012, ADR-0014.

docs.title: 3. The original is delivered whenever it can be
docs.text:
The preferred outcome is the file as it is, then the same tracks in another container, then a transcode of only the tracks that need it. Quality is not something the viewer has to choose before playing: the server keeps the source's quality unless a real constraint (the device, the connection, a limit) prevents it.

See How playback is decided.

docs.title: 4. Decisions rest on what was proved, not on names
docs.text:
A player's capabilities come from what its device reports, not from a list of known devices. A graphics card is used for what it passed during measurement, not for what its model should support. When a capability cannot be proved, the server takes the conservative answer: an unknown cast receiver gets the capabilities of the oldest one, and pixel formats players do not yet report follow a fixed compatibility rule. Assuming too much gives a black screen or wrong colours; assuming too little costs a transcode.

See Casting, Hardware acceleration, ADR-0029.

docs.title: 5. One playback, one decision
docs.text:
A playback is decided once, when it starts, and every manifest and segment of the session is served from that decision. The player never receives segments from two encodings, and what Stream info reports is derived from the same serving plan the playback pipeline uses, checked by tests in both directions.

See Playback pipeline, ADR-0030, ADR-0024.

docs.title: 6. The server sizes itself to the machine
docs.text:
The server measures how much it can transcode and admits no more: a small machine plays fewer transcoded streams, rather than playing all of them badly. Playback comes first; background work pauses while someone watches. The same image runs on a NAS and on a server with several graphics cards.

See Transcoding and server capacity, Background work and server load.

docs.title: 7. Few settings, each in one place
docs.text:
What must exist before the server starts (storage, secrets, the public address) is in the compose file; everything that can change later is in the admin panel, stored in the database, and applies without a restart wherever nothing requires it. Detection and measurement replace settings wherever they can: an installation is one compose file, libraries and users.

See Install, Configuration reference, ADR-0028.

docs.title: Decision records
docs.text: Structural choices are recorded as architecture decision records, with the context, the options weighed and the consequences. They are kept with the code: docs/adr.

docs.title: Languages & Accessibility
docs.text: Where Evey stands on internationalization (i18n) and accessibility (a11y): what is translated and how the catalogue reaches each client, then what is in place for assistive technology and what is not. The catalogue lives in i18n/<locale>/*.yaml at the repository root, served by internal/pkg/i18n and loaded by each app's i18n module. This is a self-hosted project maintained by one person: treat a11y in particular as best-effort, not certified.

docs.title: What is and is not translated
docs.text:
Translated by Evey Not translated by Evey the UI chrome: buttons, menus, settings, error messages, push notification text, notification e-mails (in the recipient's language) media metadata (titles, plot summaries, genres), which comes from the metadata provider in the Metadata language set in the setup wizard or in Admin → Server Config → Language & Region (EVEY_METADATA_LANGUAGE is only the default) your own libraries, file names, and anything you type, stored as-is

Password reset e-mails are sent in English. The UI language and the metadata language are two separate settings: the UI can be in French while a film's synopsis is in English, or the reverse.

docs.title: Supported UI languages
docs.text: Six: English (en), French (fr), German (de), Spanish (es), Chinese (zh), Hindi (hi). English is the source language and the fallback: any string missing in another language falls back to English rather than showing a blank or a key.

docs.title: How a string reaches the screen
docs.text:
• One source of truth: /i18n/<locale>/*.yaml at the repo root, split into namespaces (common, auth, media, player, admin, errors, notifications, mobile, downloads, requests). The same catalogue drives every surface.
  • The server loads it and serves it at GET /api/v1/i18n/{locale}, and uses it directly for translated API error messages and notification text.
  • The web app loads translations from that endpoint (i18next with the HTTP backend), keeps a copy in the browser's local storage for the next start, and keeps <html lang> in sync with the active language so assistive tech announces the right language. The mobile and TV apps load from the same endpoint through the shared native i18n module and ship a bundled English floor (fallback.en.json, offlineStrings.ts) for the screens shown before a server answers.
  • Language is picked from your account preference, falling back to the browser/device language (Accept-Language is parsed, region stripped: fr-FR becomes fr), then to the Server language of Admin → Server Config → Language & Region (which also sets the language of new accounts), then to English.
  • Interpolation and pluralization use i18next ({{count}} etc.).

docs.title: What is not done yet
docs.text:
• Completeness varies. English is authoritative and always complete; the other five are kept at parity by hand, with a test (internal/pkg/i18n/parity_test.go) that fails when a key set drifts, but a brand-new feature may land in English first and fall back until translated.
  • No right-to-left languages. There is no Arabic/Hebrew/Persian, and the layout has not been built or tested for RTL: adding one is real work (CSS logical properties, dir handling), not just a translation file.
  • Translations are not professionally reviewed. They are maintainer quality. Corrections are welcome.
  • Locale-aware formatting is partial. Dates and numbers rely on the platform Intl/browser locale and are not uniformly wired on every screen.

docs.title: Adding or fixing a language
docs.text:
1. Copy i18n/en/ to i18n/<your-locale>/ and translate the YAML values (keep the keys).
  2. Add the locale to the allowlist in internal/pkg/i18n/i18n.go (supportedLocales).
  3. Keep the key set identical across locales: the parity test fails otherwise, and TestI18nPlaceholdersAgreeAcrossLocales checks that the {{placeholders}} of each string agree too.

docs.title: Where this stands
docs.text: Evey is built with semantic HTML, ARIA labels and React Native accessibility props, and a few things below are deliberate. But it has not been formally audited against WCAG, there is no automated accessibility testing in the suite, and it has not been systematically tested with screen readers. Parts of it are likely usable with assistive tech; parts are likely not. If you depend on AT, expect rough edges and please report specifics.

docs.title: What is in place
docs.text: Area What is done Reduced motion prefers-reduced-motion: reduce is honored globally (frontend/apps/web/src/styles/main.css): animations and transitions are effectively disabled when your OS asks for it Language for AT <html lang> tracks the active UI language Keyboard (player) full keyboard controls with an on-screen shortcuts overlay (?, KeyboardShortcutsOverlay.tsx); shortcuts are suppressed while you type in a field Labelled controls icon-only buttons and sliders carry aria-label on web and accessibilityLabel/accessibilityRole on mobile (the larger share of interactive controls, not all) Theming five themes ship in-box (default dark, AMOLED, dark-red, light-default, light-blue); more via theme plugins Android TV D-pad focus handling for remote navigation

docs.title: What is not done yet
docs.text:
• No screen-reader pass. NVDA/VoiceOver/TalkBack flows are unverified; some custom widgets (menus, modals, the seek bar, track pickers) may not announce their state or role correctly.
  • Focus management is not audited. Focus-visible styling and focus order in dialogs and overlays are inconsistent in places.
  • Contrast is measured for the built-in themes only. A unit test (frontend/packages/theme/src/contrast.test.ts) holds every shipped theme to WCAG AA 4.5:1 for the accent, the three text ramps and the danger set against the background and both surfaces; the TV app re-checks its derived tokens (ThemeProvider.contrast.test.ts). Theme plugins and the colours a plugin injects at runtime are not checked: a custom theme can still fail in spots. AAA is not targeted.
  • No in-app text scaling beyond browser/OS zoom, and no dedicated high-contrast mode.
  • Subtitle styling on mobile is limited (a constraint of the underlying expo-video player), though subtitle/caption tracks themselves play.

docs.title: Reporting an issue
docs.text: Tell us the page/screen, the specific control, what you expected, and the assistive tech + version you used. Concrete reports get fixed; "it's not accessible" cannot be acted on. a11y fixes are handled best-effort.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Evey runs as one container: the image serves the API and the web interface on one port, and runs its own database (Postgres) and search engine (Meilisearch) inside it. This page is for the person who runs Docker at home or on a NAS: copy the compose file, start it, open http://<server-address>:9091 in a browser, and continue with the setup wizard. No .env, no privileged mode, no memory or CPU setting.

Not the repository's docker-compose.yml

The docker-compose.yml at the root of the Git repository is a different layout (Postgres as a separate service, a bundled Caddy, a required .env). Use the file on this page. The other layout is described in Advanced deployments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Docker with Compose v2 (docker compose, not the older docker-compose).
  • A persistent disk for Evey's data (the compose file below keeps it in ./evey-data, next to the file).
  • An x86-64 host, or ARM64 with a release tag: see ARM hosts.

Evey serves plain HTTP. To reach it from outside your home over HTTPS, put a reverse proxy in front of it later: see Remote access and HTTPS.

docs.title: The compose file
docs.text:
Save this as docker-compose.yml and replace the media path on the last volume line.

docker-compose.yml
services:
  evey:
    image: eveyproject/evey:beta-0.0.1 # (1)!
    container_name: evey-server
    ports:
      - "9091:9091" # (2)!
    volumes:
      - ./evey-data:/data # (3)!
      - evey-cache:/cache # (4)!
      - /path/to/your/media:/media # (5)!
    stop_grace_period: 60s # (6)!
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  evey-cache:
  1. Evey is in beta and has no numbered release yet, so there is no latest tag: beta-0.0.1 follows the development branch and moves with every change. To run the same code from one pull to the next, put an immutable sha-<commit> tag here instead: see Backups and updates.
