  2. The API and the web interface, on one port, in plain HTTP. The number on the left is the port you will type in the browser and in the apps; keep 9091 unless it is already taken on the host.
  3. Everything Evey owns: database, signing key, generated passwords, search index, timeline thumbnails, artwork, logs, backups, plugins. This is the folder to back up.
  4. Transcoding cache: segments, resized photos and covers. It can be deleted at any time and refills on demand.
  5. Your media. Mounted read-write on purpose: the repairs of Media health rewrite files in place. Append :ro for a read-only library and those repairs will fail. More folders are mounted as /media2, /media3...
  6. Leaves the embedded database time to stop cleanly on docker stop. Docker's default of 10 seconds is short for a large catalogue.

docs.title: First launch
docs.text:
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f evey

On the first start the server generates its signing key and passwords in ./evey-data, creates the database and applies its migrations. Nothing has to be prepared by hand.

docs.title: The address to open next
docs.text:
Open http://<server-address>:9091 in a browser on the same network:

Where the browser is Address to type On the machine running Docker http://localhost:9091 Another computer or a phone at home http:// + the IP of the Docker host on your home network + :9091, for example http://192.168.1.20:9091 Outside your home Not yet: this needs HTTPS and a public address, see Remote access and HTTPS

The IP of the Docker host is in your router's list of devices, or on the host itself (ip a on Linux, ipconfig on Windows, ifconfig on macOS). The port is the left-hand number of the ports: line in the compose file.

A server with no administrator opens on the setup wizard: continue with First setup. Once the administrator exists, the same address opens on the sign-in page.

The apps ask for the same address

The Android and Android TV apps ask for the server address on their first screen. It is exactly this address, with http:// and the port: The server address to enter.

docs.title: Where the data lives
docs.text: Location Contains Can be deleted? ./evey-data Database, signing key, generated passwords, search index, timeline thumbnails, artwork, logs, backups, plugins No. Losing it loses every account, watch history and setting. Only meili/ inside it can go: the search index is rebuilt from the database with evey admin reindex-search. evey-cache volume Transcoded segments, resized photos and covers Yes. Regenerated on demand. Your media folders Your files Evey does not delete them; removing a title in Evey removes it from the library, not from the disk. It writes there in three cases: a repair run from Media health (the original is kept as a backup), subtitles downloaded from OpenSubtitles (a .subtitles folder next to the film), and a probe file of a few seconds that checks the folder watcher still receives events.

docs.title: Common variations
docs.text:
Each of these is a few lines added to the same file.

A second media folder. Add - /other/path:/media2 under volumes:.

Another port on the host. Change the left-hand number only, for example "8080:9091", and type :8080 in the browser and the apps instead.

File ownership. By default the container adopts the owner of your /media mount, so that repairs can write. To choose it yourself, set PUID and PGID under environment: (the output of id -u and id -g). The container starts as root only to apply that mapping; the server itself never runs as root.

A graphics card for transcoding. Map the device into the container: see Hardware acceleration.

Behind a reverse proxy you already run. See Remote access and HTTPS.

On a NAS (Synology Container Manager, QNAP Container Station)
  • Create the evey-data folder before the first start. These interfaces refuse a bind mount whose folder does not exist, unlike the Docker command line. Nothing else needs creating.
  • Set PUID and PGID to the NAS user that owns the media (id <user> over SSH; on Synology typically around 1026, group 100). A NAS share is often owned by root, which the automatic detection never adopts.
  • Intel NAS with Quick Sync: add the devices: and group_add: lines described in Hardware acceleration.

docs.title: What you do not need to configure
docs.text: Transcoding capacity, the graphics card, the playback method for each device and remote access are decided by the server: it measures the machine on its first quiet moment, detects the hardware you mapped, and opens remote access when you give it a public address. Settings that can change later (server name, schedules, limits, API keys) are in the admin panel, not in the compose file. The environment variables that do exist are listed in the Configuration reference.

docs.title: E-mail and notifications
docs.text: Evey tells each profile when new films, series, seasons, episodes or albums arrive, in the apps and, once e-mail is set up, by e-mail. This page is for the administrator who sets up the mail server and for anyone choosing what their profile receives. Administrators also hear about failed backups, plugin errors and new media requests, and whoever made a request hears back when it is answered.

docs.title: Where notifications appear
docs.text:
• In every app: the bell, with an unread count. Always on, nothing to set up. A notification is kept 30 days. The list only shows titles from libraries the account can open.
  • Browser push: on the web, each profile turns on Push Notifications in Settings → Notifications, once per browser. The server creates its push keys on first start; see E-mail and notifications to bring your own. Browsers allow push only on an HTTPS address (or localhost); elsewhere the setting says Push notifications need an HTTPS address: open this server over HTTPS to turn them on. The Android and TV apps do not receive push notifications.
  • E-mail: once e-mail is set up, every notification is also sent to the account's address, in the profile's language, with a link to the server. An account with several profiles receives one e-mail per event. There is no per-user opt-out.

docs.title: Set up e-mail
docs.text:
Admin → Server Config → Email / SMTP:

Field Value SMTP Host, Port The mail server. 587 with starttls or 465 with ssl are the usual pairs. Username, Password The account to sign in with. From Address The sender address of every message. TLS Mode starttls upgrades a plain connection, ssl uses TLS from the start, none sends without encryption.

Save SMTP Settings applies at once, without a restart. Send test email sends a short message to your own account's address with the saved settings, and shows the mail server's answer when it fails.

The EVEY_SMTP_* variables are the fallback, used while the card has no host:

.env
EVEY_SMTP_HOST=smtp.example.com
EVEY_SMTP_PORT=587
EVEY_SMTP_USERNAME=notifications@example.com
EVEY_SMTP_PASSWORD=your-smtp-password
EVEY_SMTP_FROM=noreply@example.com
EVEY_SMTP_TLS=starttls

One source at a time

As soon as a host is saved in the card, every field comes from the card and the variables are ignored, so the server never sends the variables' credentials to a mail server typed in the panel. Clear the host to go back to the variables.

E-mail is used for notifications and password resets; invitations are links you share yourself.

docs.title: Choose what a profile receives
docs.text:
In Settings → Notifications, each profile picks a level for Movies, Series and Music:

Level New titles notified All Every one. The default. Relevant Only those sharing a genre with the profile's usual genres. Important only Currently the same as Relevant. Disabled None.

A genre counts as usual when it appears in at least 3 of the profile's last 200 playbacks. A title without genres is never notified at the Relevant and Important only levels.

Several episodes of one series arriving within 24 hours make a single notification that counts them, and none is sent when the series or the season was just announced.

docs.title: Let people reset their password
docs.text:
1. Set up e-mail (above).
  2. Turn on Password recovery in Admin → Server Config → Server Settings. It applies immediately.
  3. The sign-in page then shows Forgot your password?, which e-mails a reset link.

Without a mail server the link stays hidden, even with the option on.

docs.title: Single sign-on (OIDC)
docs.text: Let people sign in with the identity provider you already run (Keycloak, Authentik, Authelia, Google or any other OpenID Connect provider): the sign-in page of the web and Android apps then shows Sign in with SSO next to the password form. Two steps for the administrator: register Evey at the provider, then fill one card in the admin panel.

docs.title: 1. Register Evey with the provider
docs.text:
Create a client (or application) in the provider with the Authorization Code grant, the scopes openid email profile, a client secret, and the two addresses the Single sign-on (SSO) card shows under Register these addresses at your provider:

Field Value Redirect URI https://<your address>/api/v1/auth/oidc/callback Post-logout redirect URI https://<your address>/login

Both are built from the server's public address (Admin → Remote Access): set that first if people reach Evey under another address.

docs.title: 2. Configure Evey
docs.text:
Admin → Server Config → Single sign-on (SSO):

Field Effect Enable single sign-on Shows the SSO button on the sign-in screens. Issuer URL The provider's address; Evey reads /.well-known/openid-configuration under it. Client ID, Client secret The client registered above. The secret is kept on the server and never shown again; leaving the dots keeps it. Allowed e-mail domains Comma separated. When set, only these addresses are accepted, and the provider must confirm the address. Button label Optional, replaces "Sign in with SSO". Link to existing accounts by verified e-mail On by default. See Who can sign in. Create accounts for new SSO users Off unless e-mail domains are allowed. See Who can sign in. Library access for new SSO accounts All libraries, or Only the selected libraries.

Test connection checks that the issuer answers. Save SSO settings applies at once, without a restart. The Status line says whether the provider is reachable, with the last error if it is not.

The EVEY_OIDC_* variables of Accounts and sign-in are the fallback: the card says when its values come from them, and saving the card takes over.

The provider is never on the server's critical path

The server starts even when the provider is down, the SSO button stays hidden while the provider cannot be reached, and password sign-in keeps working. The provider is contacted again on the next sign-in attempt, at most every 30 seconds.

docs.title: Who can sign in
docs.text:
1. An account that already signed in with this provider signs in again, unless it is disabled.
  2. Otherwise, with Link to existing accounts by verified e-mail on, an existing account with the same e-mail is linked to the provider and signed in, but only when the provider confirms the address. The account keeps its password. Administrator accounts are never linked this way.
  3. Otherwise, with Create accounts for new SSO users on, a new account is created, with one profile and the library access chosen in the card. Its username is the provider's preferred_username, otherwise the part of the e-mail before @; a name already taken gets a short suffix.

Why account creation is off by default

With a public provider such as Google, anyone holding an account there could otherwise get one on your server. Creation is on by default only when Allowed e-mail domains restricts who qualifies. When it is off, only existing accounts can sign in with SSO.

When a sign-in is refused, the sign-in page says why: the e-mail domain is not allowed, no account matches and sign-up is off, the account is disabled, the account exists but could not be linked, or the provider is unavailable.

docs.title: Signing out
docs.text: When the provider publishes a logout endpoint, signing out of Evey after an SSO sign-in also ends the session at the provider, then returns to the Evey sign-in page. The card says whether the provider supports it.

docs.title: Serving a video - the HLS playback path
docs.text: What happens when a player asks for a video, from the first master.m3u8 request down to the bytes of a segment: the read path. The code is spread across the http driving adapter (internal/adapters/driving/http/transcode_*), the app/transcoding services and the ffmpeg / mkvgo / prober driven adapters; no single function runs the whole flow, so this page is the map. It is decided by ADR-0030 (one plan, one decision), ADR-0024 (the plan resolver) and ADR-0029 (measured capabilities). It is the counterpart of the scan pipeline in Architecture and the deep dive behind "Golden path 4" of the Codebase map. For the user-facing view of the same negotiation, read How playback is decided.

docs.title: The mental model: 3 questions, 2 engines, 1 key
docs.text:
Serving a video reduces to answering three questions, then packaging the answer, with everything addressed by one hash.

Question Answered by Where Q1 - Can I read the file cheaply? probe dispatch by file extension: .mkv/.webm and .mp4/.mov go to mkvgo (head-only, no process); everything else, and any fast-path failure, goes to ffprobe, the authority adapters/driven/prober/dispatcher.go Q2 - Can the client play it as-is? the playback decision, taken per track: video copy vs transcode, audio copy vs transcode vs the wasm AC-3 path; video and audio are decided independently, and the common case is "copy the video, re-encode the audio to AAC" app/transcoding/decision.go Q3 - How much can this host encode? the calibrated capability (measured at the first quiet moment) plus admission (which ladder rung fits, is there a slot) app/transcoding/calibration_service.go, admission_shaper.go

Two engines run through all of it:

  • mkvgo reads and repackages (remux, on-demand) without spawning a process. Free.
  • ffmpeg / ffprobe decode, re-encode and probe by spawning a process. Costly.

One key: everything (cache directory, ffmpeg session, segment URLs) is addressed by the decision fingerprint, a hash of the decision. Same bytes, same hash, one shared encode. The whole system's correctness rests on that hash being stable between the manifest a player holds and every segment it later fetches.

flowchart LR
    req[Player request<br/>master / variant / segment / audio]
    h[http adapter<br/>transcode_handler_vod.go<br/>auth, dispatch]
    plan[PlanResolver<br/>app/transcoding<br/>decision + capability + ladder<br/>+ route + fingerprint]
    mkv[mkvgo<br/>copy rung, no process]
    ff[ffmpeg<br/>transcode, tonemap]
    pack[Manifests<br/>master.m3u8, stream_N.m3u8,<br/>manifest.mpd]
    seg[(cache/transcode/segments/hash)]
    req --> h --> plan
    plan -->|copy| mkv
    plan -->|transcode| ff
    plan --> pack
    mkv --> seg
    ff --> seg

docs.title: Reading order - follow one request through the code
docs.text:
Open these in sequence to trace a single playback request end to end:

  1. Entry - internal/adapters/driving/http/transcode_handler_vod.go: serveHTTP authenticates, then dispatches to master / variant / segment / audio.
  2. The plan - http/transcode_vod_plan.go marshals the *http.Request into a transport-free PlaybackRequest; app/transcoding/playback_plan_resolver.go (PlanResolver.Resolve, the concrete PlaybackPlanResolver in playback_plan.go) returns one immutable PlaybackPlan: the decision (Q2), the ladder class, the shaped ladder, the hardware route, the packager and the fingerprint. Every manifest and segment of the session is served from it: manifest input, shed probe, stale-URL seal, producer pick and segment key all read that single resolution, so within a request the cache-hash invariant holds by construction (the segment hot path went from about 5 profile-preference fetches to 1). The source-fact helpers (codec, HDR, SAR, ten-bit...) live alongside in source_facts.go. makeDecision and buildFingerprint in http/transcode_vod_fingerprint.go are thin wrappers for the call sites without a plan (prewarm, on-demand master).
  3. Q2 - Decision - internal/app/transcoding/decision.go: MakePlaybackDecisionWithPrefs (pure) is the per-track copy/transcode brain. The resolver layers on the request-time pins (vd= / ad=), the audio-resync override, etc.
  4. Q3 - Capability - internal/app/transcoding/calibration_service.go: Current() returns domain/transcoding.Derive(report, policy) (derive.go), the host's ceilings derived from the last calibration.
  5. Ladder and admission - the resolver shapes the ladder (complexity class, producer profiles, source/capability caps, CMCD/AV1 caps, admission route and ceiling), then freezes it on the admission pin (admission_shaper.go, FreezeLadder), read verbatim on every later call: the cache-hash invariant made structural. video_session_limiter.go holds the capacity slot; the route spills from hardware to software when full.
  6. Fingerprint - a DecisionFingerprint (type and Hash() in app/transcoding/segment_cache.go), assembled by the resolver. The hash is the cache key.
  7. Producing the bytes - copy: mkvgo, app/transcoding/ondemand.go (port) and adapters/driven/mkvgo/ondemand.go; transcode: ffmpeg, adapters/driven/ffmpeg/hls_transcoder.go (BuildFFmpegArgs is pure; segments land in /cache/transcode/segments/<hash>/).
  8. Packaging - app/transcoding/manifest_generator.go writes master.m3u8 / stream_N.m3u8; manifest_generator_dash.go writes manifest.mpd.

Across requests, the invariant rests on URL baking

Every input to the decision must be baked into the child URLs (querySuffix in manifest_generator.go), or a mid-play poll can flip the plan under the player. Per-session URLs are re-baked (transcode_vod_manifest_rebake.go) to carry the stream token, for HLS and DASH alike, including cookie-less Chromecast.

docs.title: The two engines, by cost
docs.text:
The probe dispatcher (adapters/driven/prober/dispatcher.go) is a chain of responsibility keyed on extension: it tries mkvgo, and falls back to ffprobe on any doubt (parse error, panic, unmappable result, a dropped MP4 media track, DoVi profile 5, unreadable colour). Both fast paths are always on (nil gates in wire.go); ffprobe is the safety net, never bypassed. A second, identical dispatcher (keyframe_dispatcher.go) handles the seek index.

Operation mkvgo (free) ffprobe / ffmpeg (costly) Metadata probe (codec, dims, HDR, bitrate, duration) .mkv/.webm/.mp4/.mov head-only everything else, or fallback Frame-rate mode (cfr/vfr) AnalyzeFrameRateMode - Remux MKV to MP4 (no re-encode) RemuxToMP4 - On-demand HLS/DASH (copy rung) OnDemandPackager - Video re-encode / HDR tonemap - hls_transcoder.go Interlace detect (idet), seek-landing, chromaprint, DoVi P5 - (needs decode / side-data) ffmpeg / ffprobe

Three ffprobe forks still run on MKV/MP4 sources whose data mkvgo already exposes, all in the ffmpeg driven adapter: the duration in trickplay.go, bitrate and dimensions in complexity_classifier.go, the playback audio delay in audio_delay.go.

docs.title: Audio is decided separately from video
docs.text:
makeDecision produces VideoDecision and AudioDecision independently. The "copy rung" (isCopyRequest) is gated on the video only; even a copied video usually carries a re-encoded AAC track alongside. The audio decision has three outcomes:

Outcome What is served copy the source track as is transcode to AAC ffmpeg, light the wasm path, for AC-3 / E-AC-3 on a browser that cannot decode it natively the master is made video-only with an #EVEY-AUDIO-URI tag, the AC-3 is copied (mkvgo od_audio if the plan builds, else ffmpeg -c:a copy), and ac3go.wasm decodes it to PCM in the browser (WasmAudioEngine.ts), clock-locked to the video

Safari is excluded from the wasm path by capability, not by name: canWasmDecodeAC3() (frontend/packages/client/src/web/codec.ts) returns true only when the browser reports it cannot play AC-3 natively, and Safari reports it can.

docs.title: Packaging: CMAF, HLS, DASH
docs.text:
The container is always CMAF (fMP4): a per-variant init.mp4 plus .m4s segments (the MPEG-TS branch in hls_transcoder.go is dead: needsFMP4Segments always returns true). Over the same segments:

  • HLS (master.m3u8, stream_N.m3u8, EXT-X-MAP init + .m4s), both engines.
  • DASH (manifest.mpd): on the mkvgo copy path the packager's own manifest (OnDemandPlan.HasDASH, byte-identical, zero storage, disabled under AES-128); on the ffmpeg path a manifest declared from the plan over the same fragments the HLS playlists address (ManifestGenerator.MPD), written before any fragment exists.

What makes the DASH manifest honest is the segment grid (domain/transcoding.SegmentGrid): every transcoded rung is cut on the same whole number of frames, round(3 s x fps) (72 at 23.976 fps, 75 at 25, 90 at 29.97), so a segment is exact in the video track's ticks and identical across the switch set; the copy fallback declares its keyframe plan. A source whose frame rate is unknown or variable stays on the legacy 3 s clock, keeps HLS, and answers 404 on manifest.mpd. No client is switched to DASH: HLS stays the default everywhere. mkvgo's DASHFromCMAF over the produced fragments is the parity oracle (internal/pkg/cmafparity, TestDASHGridIntegration at 23.976/25/29.97 fps: cold, seek, two-rung switch set, separate audio within one AAC frame).

docs.title: Design patterns in play
docs.text: Pattern Where Ports and adapters (hexagonal) the app layer talks to StreamProber, BenchmarkRunner, OnDemandPackager, StreamProducer; ffmpeg and mkvgo implement them, and a new engine is a new adapter Strategy StreamProducer (software / hardware / copy), picked by a ProducerSelector Chain of responsibility with fallback the probe and keyframe dispatchers (mkvgo, then ffprobe as the authority) Content-addressed cache the DecisionFingerprint hash keys the cache and the ffmpeg session Pure core, imperative shell Derive, MakePlaybackDecision and the cost model are pure, unit-tested without ffmpeg or a database Immutable value object StreamPlan, the admission decision, emitted once and never mutated, so the URLs-to-bytes invariant holds by construction Graceful degradation a safe fallback at every step: 720p default capability, hardware-to-software spill, copy-to-transcode, mkvgo-to-ffprobe

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
This page is for the administrator: how to install a plugin or a theme, what you accept when you do, and what the server lets it touch on your host. Everything happens in Admin → Plugins; the pages for plugin authors are listed at the end.

A plugin adds to Evey what it does not do by itself: a section on the home page, an overlay in the player, a metadata source, a theme. Each plugin is a separate process that talks to the server through a local socket, confined by a sandbox and limited to the permissions its manifest declares. Its interface, when it has one, runs in an isolated frame of the page.

Without plugins. With the example weather plugin: a section at the top, drawn in its own frame.

docs.title: Install a plugin
docs.text:
1. In Admin → Plugins, open Install Plugin and choose the Plugin file (.zip). If the author ships a signature, add it in Signature file (.zip.sig, optional). The From URL tab installs from a link instead; append #sha256:<hash> to the URL to have the download checked.
  2. Preview & Install analyses the package without installing it. The preview shows the Permissions and Capabilities the plugin asks for, the slots of the interface it wants to appear in, the hosts it will contact, the result of the Static Analysis and, when the server checks signatures, whether the package is Signed.
  3. Read that list as the contract: those are the only things the plugin will be able to do. Confirm, and the plugin starts.
Admin → Plugins: the runtimes available, the resource limits, and one card per plugin.

A package whose analysis finds a critical pattern is refused, whatever you answer. Warnings are shown and left to you. The plugin's language must be among the Available Runtimes of the server: the default image ships Python only, the -nodejs image adds Node.js and the -full image adds PHP, Ruby and Lua.

Signed plugins

A plugin author can sign the ZIP with cosign, and you decide what an unsigned or badly signed plugin does. To verify signatures, give the server the author's public key and pick a policy:

EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY=/etc/evey/cosign.pub
EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_POLICY=warn      # off | warn (default) | enforce

With warn, a failed signature is shown in the preview and in the Security Dashboard; with enforce, the install or the update is refused. Nothing is verified without a public key, and the server needs no cosign binary. Authors: see Sign your plugin.

docs.title: Update a plugin
docs.text: On the plugin's card, Update from source… takes the new ZIP (a path or a URL) and shows the same preview. An update must carry a higher version than the installed one. When it asks for new permissions, capabilities, slots or hosts, the preview says This update requests new permissions and lists the difference: nothing is applied until you choose Approve and install. The package analysed is the package installed: its hash is checked again when the update is applied.

docs.title: Manage the installed plugins
docs.text:
Each card shows the plugin's state (Enabled or Disabled) and offers:

Action What it does Enabled / Disabled Starts or stops the plugin's process. A disabled plugin keeps its files and its configuration. Config The settings the plugin declares (an API key, a city, a unit...). Secret fields are shown masked and are never sent back to the browser. Logs The last lines the plugin wrote through the host. Uninstall Removes the process, the files and the plugin's stored data.

Resource limits, at the top of the page, caps every plugin process. The values in the panel are the defaults; the environment variable sets them when the panel has never been saved.

Field Default Environment variable Max memory (MiB) 256 EVEY_PLUGINS_MEMORY_MB Max processes 64 EVEY_PLUGINS_PIDS_MAX Max disk (MiB) 100 EVEY_PLUGINS_DISK_MAX_MB CPU nice (0-19) 10 EVEY_PLUGINS_CPU_NICE Sandbox mode auto EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE

Memory, processes and disk apply at the next sweep of the monitor, which stops a plugin that exceeds them; the CPU priority and the sandbox mode apply to plugins started afterwards. 0 disables a memory, process or disk limit.

The Security Dashboard keeps, per plugin, the findings of the analysis, the signature result and the last error. Its Host sandbox line shows the sandbox mode actually in force on this machine: if it reads basic, the host offers no per-path filesystem isolation, and Plugin sandbox setup explains what to change.

Plugins are enabled by default. EVEY_PLUGINS_ENABLED=false turns the whole subsystem off.

docs.title: What a plugin can do on your host
docs.text:
Whatever its manifest says, a plugin:

  • sees its own directory, not the server's data nor the media files;
  • has no direct network access: a plugin with the network permission reaches only the hosts it declared, through the server, with GET and HEAD;
  • cannot start child processes unless it declares subprocess;
  • runs under the resource limits above and, when the host allows it, under a separate user.

Its interface is confined to the slots the manifest declares: a section or the hero area of the home page, a sidebar panel in a library or on a detail page, an overlay of the player, the appearance settings, the bottom of the navigation sidebar, or one entry in the admin menu that opens the plugin's own page. A plugin can never draw into the sign-in, setup, security or existing admin screens. In its frame, it has no access to the page, your cookies or your session: what it reads from the server goes through a short-lived token limited to the two permissions it may ask for (public for a safe projection of media titles and posters, prefs for the current user's preferences in its own namespace).

The permissions a plugin can ask for are listed in Permissions and slots. How the sandbox works, and what it still cannot prevent, is in Plugin sandbox and threat model.

The server checks where a plugin talks, not what it says

Once a host is on a plugin's list, the server cannot inspect what the plugin sends to it. Review a third-party plugin before installing it, as you would any software, and treat its host list as the list of parties that may receive your library's titles.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text: A theme is a package of kind: theme with no process: a stylesheet, and optionally a script confined to a hidden frame. It is installed from the same Install Plugin dialog; the stylesheet is sanitized at install. Each user then picks it under Settings → Appearance → Theme. What a theme may contain is described in Themes.

docs.title: Writing a plugin
docs.text: Page Contents Writing a plugin A first plugin step by step, the install loop, signing, distribution. Start here. Plugin API reference The manifest, the backend calls and data store, the evey.* bridge of the interface. Permissions and slots What a manifest may declare, what is checked at install, the external fetch rules, the slots. Themes Restyling the interface with CSS and a sandboxed script. Webhooks and API keys Integrating Evey with other tools without writing a plugin.

docs.title: Privacy policy
docs.text:
Last updated: 2026-10-04.

This policy covers the Evey apps for Android and Android TV. The Evey project runs no service that receives your data: no account with us, no analytics, no advertising, no crash reporting to us. The apps talk to the Evey server that you, or the person who invited you, installed and runs.

docs.title: What the apps send, and to whom
docs.text:
To your Evey server, and to nothing else we operate. The apps send what a media player needs to work:

  • your username and password when you sign in (or the Quick Connect code), then a session token;
  • what you browse, search, play, rate, favourite or request, and your playback position, so you can resume on another device;
  • the name of the device (as Android reports it), so you can tell your devices apart in Play On and in the server's list of sessions;
  • technical playback reports: which audio and video formats the device can decode, and errors met while playing, so the server can pick a stream the device can play;
  • a picture, only when you choose one as a profile avatar, and files you pick yourself (an external subtitle, a plugin, a backup) as an administrator.

Who can read this data is up to the operator of that server. The Evey project has no access to it.

To third parties, only in these cases:

  • Posters and album art. Some pictures shown in media requests and music come straight from their public source (The Movie Database, the Cover Art Archive, IMDb). The device fetches them like a web browser would, which reveals its IP address to that host.
  • Casting. Casting to a Chromecast goes through Google Cast, part of Google Play services on your phone. The Chromecast loads the Evey receiver page from cast.eveyproject.org, hosted by GitHub Pages. The media itself streams from your server.
  • Voice search on Android TV. The microphone button hands over to the television's own voice recognizer (usually Google's). The app receives the recognized text, never the recording.
  • Links you open. A trailer, a The Movie Database or IMDb page, or the Play Store page for an update opens in the matching app or browser, under that service's own policy.
  • Plugins. Plugins are installed by the server's administrator. A plugin may show content from an outside service (a weather plugin, for instance).

docs.title: What stays on the device
docs.text: The server address, your session token (in Android's encrypted storage), your preferences, and the films and music you download for offline viewing. Removing the app removes them. Biometric unlock (fingerprint or face), when you turn it on, is handled by Android: the app only learns whether it succeeded.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Permission Why Internet, Wi-Fi state Reach your server, tell your home network apart from the outside. Camera Scan a Quick Connect QR code. Nothing is recorded or sent. Notifications, foreground service Show playback and download progress, keep playing with the screen off. Biometrics Optional app lock.

The phone app does not have the microphone permission.

docs.title: This website
docs.text: eveyproject.org is hosted by GitHub Pages, which sees the visitor's IP address. The site serves its own fonts and scripts, so the browser contacts no other service. It sets no cookie of its own and has no analytics.

docs.title: Children
docs.text: The apps are not aimed at children. Kids profiles are set up by the server's operator, who holds that data.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: Questions about this policy: contact@eveyproject.org. For data held on an Evey server, contact the person who runs that server.

docs.title: Reverse proxy configurations
docs.text: Evey serves the API and the web interface together on port 9091, in plain HTTP; a reverse proxy only has to terminate TLS and forward everything to evey:9091. Pick your proxy below (bundled Caddy, Nginx, Traefik, Nginx Proxy Manager, or one you already run), then read the two sections at the end if you tune streaming or set your own security headers.

docs.title: Tell Evey about the proxy
docs.text:
Whatever the proxy, Evey needs its public address and which proxy to trust. The place for both is Admin → Remote Access: an https:// External URL and, when the proxy is a container, its network in Trusted proxies. Both apply without a restart. An https:// address is what tells Evey a proxy terminates TLS in front of it: cookies get the Secure flag, HSTS is sent and X-Forwarded-Proto from a trusted proxy is believed. The remote-access switch and the real client address are explained in Remote access and HTTPS.

The same answers can come from the environment, for an installation described entirely as code (the panel wins when both are set):

.env
EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL=https://media.example.com
EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES=172.16.0.0/12       # only needed if the proxy is a container; loopback is always trusted

The former EVEY_FORWARDED_PROTO is still accepted as an override but deprecated: the scheme of the address is enough.

Every bundled example reads the domain from one place, EVEY_DOMAIN in your .env. Set it once; Caddy, Nginx and Traefik all pick it up.

.env
EVEY_DOMAIN=media.example.com

docs.title: Files
docs.text: docker/Caddyfile, built into an image by docker/Dockerfile.caddy; the caddy service in the repository's docker-compose.yml.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
1. Set EVEY_DOMAIN in .env and make sure ports 80 and 443 of the host reach the Caddy container.
  2. Add the caddy service from the repository compose file to yours and run docker compose up -d. Caddy obtains a Let's Encrypt certificate for EVEY_DOMAIN on its own.
  3. In Admin → Remote Access, set the https:// External URL and 172.16.0.0/12 in Trusted proxies.

docs.title: What it already handles
docs.text: Proxies everything to evey:9091, with the streaming paths flushed without buffering and without a timeout. Curates the security headers and the canonical CSP of the security section and strips the app's own CSP so exactly one reaches the browser; the two pages that carry their own policy keep it.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: examples/nginx/evey.conf.template and a ready compose overlay, examples/nginx/docker-compose.nginx.yml.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
1. Set EVEY_DOMAIN in .env. The nginx image renders the template at startup with EVEY_DOMAIN substituted.
  2. Put the certificate and key where the template expects them, under the matching file names (/etc/ssl/certs/<domain>.pem, /etc/ssl/private/<domain>.key in the nginx-certs volume): the overlay does not obtain certificates for you.
  3. docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f examples/nginx/docker-compose.nginx.yml up -d.
  4. In Admin → Remote Access, set the https:// External URL and 172.16.0.0/12 in Trusted proxies.

docs.title: What it already handles
docs.text: Proxies to evey:9091 with buffering and timeouts off on the streaming paths, the SyncPlay WebSocket upgraded, X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto forwarded, and client_max_body_size 2G for plugin uploads and backup restores. It passes the app's own security headers and CSP through.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: examples/traefik/docker-compose.traefik.yml.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
1. Run Traefik with a websecure entrypoint, a letsencrypt certificate resolver and an external Docker network named proxy; the overlay labels assume those names.

  2. Set EVEY_DOMAIN in .env, then:

    docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f examples/traefik/docker-compose.traefik.yml up -d

  3. In Admin → Remote Access, set the https:// External URL and the proxy network's range in Trusted proxies (172.16.0.0/12 covers Docker's default networks).

docs.title: What it already handles
docs.text: The overlay only adds the router labels and joins the proxy network. Traefik on its defaults neither buffers responses nor caps a response's duration, so no streaming tuning is needed; it forwards X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto on its own and passes the app's security headers through.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: None: everything is set in NPM's interface. The evey container must be on the network NPM uses, see A proxy you already run.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
In Edit Proxy Host:

  1. Details: Scheme http, Forward Hostname evey-server, Forward Port 9091. Websockets Support: on (SyncPlay). Cache Assets: off - it would cache media segments and playlists with a fixed expiry. Block Common Exploits can stay on (turn it off if a search or a plugin upload ever answers 403 for no reason).
  2. SSL: your certificate, Force SSL, HTTP/2. HSTS is optional here - the app already sends it.
  3. In Admin → Remote Access, set the https:// External URL and the NPM network's range in Trusted proxies.

docs.title: What it already handles
docs.text:
NPM forwards X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto and the Host header on its own, and its default timeouts never fire on Evey's streams. Nothing else is required.

Optional - keep NPM from buffering direct-play files through its own disk: Advanced → Custom Nginx Configuration (the Custom Locations tab cannot express the regex):

# Plugin uploads (up to 100 MB) and backup restores (up to 2 GB).
client_max_body_size 2G;

# Streaming - no buffering, no timeout.
location ~ ^/api/v1/media/.+/(hls|stream) {
    proxy_pass http://evey-server:9091;
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_request_buffering off;
    proxy_read_timeout 0;
    proxy_send_timeout 0;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Connection "";
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
}

# Library scans stream their progress for as long as the scan runs.
location ~ ^/api/v1/libraries/.+/scan {
    proxy_pass http://evey-server:9091;
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_read_timeout 0;
    proxy_send_timeout 0;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Connection "";
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
}

Every other path (the web UI, the rest of the API, the SyncPlay WebSocket) goes through NPM's own proxy block, which the Details tab configures. Skip the snippet and nothing breaks - it only changes where big files are buffered.

docs.title: A proxy you already run (TLS terminated upstream)
docs.text: On a NAS that already has a reverse proxy (the vendor's, Nginx Proxy Manager, a Traefik on a shared Docker network), no Caddy is needed: Evey emits its own security headers and a complete CSP, and the streaming rules can only be enforced by the proxy that faces the client anyway. A second proxy behind it adds nothing.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
Put the evey service on that proxy's network and target evey-server:9091 (the container name; the service name evey resolves too):

docker-compose.yml
services:
  evey:
    # no ports: the proxy is the only way in
    environment:
      EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL: https://media.example.com
      EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES: 172.16.0.0/12     # narrow to the proxy's subnet once known
    # ...
networks:
  default:
    name: proxy-net
    external: true

Then, in that proxy, for the route to evey-server:9091: forward X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto, enable WebSocket support, and apply the streaming rules below on the streaming paths - the Nginx and Nginx Proxy Manager sections above show the exact lines.

docs.title: What it already handles
docs.text: That depends on the proxy: check that exactly one CSP header reaches the browser (next sections) and run evey admin doctor once the trusted proxies are set.

docs.title: Streaming - what a proxy's defaults do to it
docs.text:
Evey works behind a reverse proxy left on its defaults: every long-lived response either sends bytes continuously (HLS segments, direct play, transcode output) or pings the client every 30 s (the event streams), so a default read timeout never fires. Two things are still worth knowing:

  • Buffering. A proxy that buffers responses (nginx does by default) reads a direct-play file into its own buffers and temp files before the client gets it - functional, but a multi-GB film then transits through the proxy host's disk. proxy_buffering off on the streaming paths avoids that.
  • Scans. /api/v1/libraries/*/scan streams progress for as long as the scan runs; a proxy that caps a response's total duration (rare - nginx, Caddy and Traefik do not by default) would cut it short. The scan itself continues server-side regardless.

The paths concerned:

/api/v1/media/*/hls/*
/api/v1/media/*/stream
/api/v1/libraries/*/scan

The bundled Caddy and the Nginx example set both (no buffering, no timeout) on these paths. The Traefik example and a UI-driven proxy such as Nginx Proxy Manager keep their defaults, which are fine; the NPM snippet above is optional.

docs.title: Security headers & CSP - read this if your proxy sets its own
docs.text:
Evey emits a complete Content-Security-Policy. If your proxy passes it through, you are done.

Many setups instead strip it (header_down -Content-Security-Policy in Caddy) and curate their own - that is fine, but then your policy must keep these tokens or features break silently:

Token Directive Breaks without it 'self' frame-src Every plugin UI and theme script (blank iframe). They run in /plugin-frame.html, a page of Evey framed by the app (see below). 'wasm-unsafe-eval' script-src Browser AC-3/E-AC-3 playback (the ac3go WebAssembly decoder cannot compile, so the film plays muted). This is the narrow token that permits Wasm compilation only, not general eval(). https://www.gstatic.com script-src (+ frame-src) The Google Cast sender SDK never loads, so nobody gets a cast button. It is the only way a browser can discover Chromecasts on the user's own LAN. blob: media-src MSE playback (hls.js attaches the stream via a blob URL). blob: worker-src hls.js silently falls back to main-thread demuxing (choppier on mobile).

A known-good policy for a curating proxy, the one the bundled Caddy sends:

default-src 'self'; base-uri 'self'; object-src 'none';
img-src 'self' https: data: blob:; media-src 'self' blob:;
style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval' https://www.gstatic.com;
connect-src 'self' https: wss:; worker-src 'self' blob:; font-src 'self' data:;
frame-src 'self' https://www.gstatic.com

base-uri and object-src have no fallback to default-src, so a policy that omits them leaves <base href> injection and <object>/<embed> embedding unrestricted. Keep them if you curate your own policy. script-src has no 'unsafe-inline': a script injected into the page does not run. Do not add it back - nothing in the app needs it.

Two pages carry their own policy, sent by the app; leave the app's header on those two paths:

  • /plugin-frame.html, the page plugin UIs and theme scripts run in. Its policy sandboxes it (even opened outside an iframe), limits its network to the hosts the plugin's manifest declares, and lets only the app frame it, so it also sends X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN: do not overwrite that with DENY on this path, or every plugin UI stays blank.
  • /cast-receiver.html, the page a Chromecast loads when it plays from Evey. The Cast player injects styles, fonts and images from www.gstatic.com into it. Leave the app's header on that path, or apply this policy to that path only:
default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'wasm-unsafe-eval' https://www.gstatic.com; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://www.gstatic.com; img-src 'self' data: https: blob:; media-src 'self' blob: https:; worker-src 'self' blob:; font-src 'self' data: https://www.gstatic.com; connect-src 'self' https: wss:; frame-src https://www.gstatic.com; base-uri 'self'; object-src 'none'

Exactly one CSP header must reach the browser

With two (the app's and your proxy's, or Caddy's and Nginx Proxy Manager's "Advanced" snippet), browsers enforce the intersection: the strictest wins and the failure is silent. Check with curl -sI https://your.domain | grep -ci content-security-policy, which must print 1.

Two more checks after any change:

  • Keep the policy on one line. A CSP split across lines in a proxy config is a classic silent corruption: the join swallows the characters at the seam (...gstatic.com; connect-src became ...gstaticonnect-src once, which disabled the Cast SDK and merged two directives).
  • The plugin frame keeps its own policy: curl -sI https://your.domain/plugin-frame.html | grep -i -e content-security -e x-frame must show sandbox allow-scripts and SAMEORIGIN.

docs.title: Real client IPs and the remote-access gate
docs.text:
Once the proxy forwards the real client address, Evey can tell a viewer at home from one on the internet: that is what Max Remote Bitrate and the remote-access switch act on. Two rules:

  • The trusted proxies (panel or EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES) must cover the proxy: 172.16.0.0/12 when it is a container on the Docker network, nothing to add when it runs on the host, since loopback is always trusted and whatever you set is added to it.
  • Chained proxies each need to preserve X-Forwarded-For. In Caddy that is servers { trusted_proxies static private_ranges }; nginx uses proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;.

Turning this on changes who counts as remote: a server whose remote access was off starts refusing real remote clients (403 {"code":"remote_access_disabled"}) although no application setting changed. Evey opens remote access on its own when a public address is set and no choice was made, logs the state at every boot and each refusal with the client address, and evey admin doctor fails on "published but refusing". The whole mechanism is described in Remote access and HTTPS.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text: A theme restyles Evey's interface: a package of kind: theme with no backend process, made of a stylesheet and, optionally, a script confined to a hidden frame. This page is for theme authors; it says what the two files may contain and what the installer rewrites or refuses. Themes are installed like plugins, from Admin → Plugins, and each user picks one under Settings → Appearance → Theme.

docs.title: Manifest
docs.text:
plugin.yaml
name: aurora               # required; human-readable name
version: 1.0.0             # required; semver
kind: theme                # required

description: "..."         # optional
author: "..."              # optional

# no language, entrypoint, permissions or capabilities: the install is refused

The ZIP holds theme.css and/or theme.js at its root, next to the manifest. A package with neither is accepted and has no visible effect. examples/plugins/theme-dark-blue (a short theme.css overriding the colour variables) and examples/plugins/open-workshop (a complete restyle) both pass the sanitizer and are good starting points.

docs.title: theme.css
docs.text: The stylesheet is injected as a <link rel="stylesheet"> in the head of every page and applies to the whole document: custom properties, @keyframes, @media, @font-face with data: sources, @layer and container queries all work. It is served at /api/v1/themes/<id>/theme.css without authentication, so a theme the browser remembers applies before sign-in too.

docs.title: Start from the custom properties
docs.text:
The interface draws its surfaces, text, accent, borders and radii from a set of custom properties on :root; examples/plugins/theme-dark-blue/theme.css lists them with a comment each. Overriding them restyles every screen at once:

theme.css
:root {
  --bg: #0b1120;
  --surface: #162032;
  --text: #e2e8f0;
  --accent: #3b82f6;
  --accent-hover: #60a5fa;
  --radius: 8px;
}

docs.title: Stable theming hooks
docs.text:
A few cosmetic elements carry stable classes you can target without depending on the utility classes, which change between releases. These are a contract: they will not be renamed.

Selector Element Safe to restyle .evey-app-header the top bar colours, height, spacing, blur; never hide or move the controls inside it .evey-media-grid the media card grids (library, rows) columns, gap, alignment .evey-media-card one media card (poster and meta) width, spacing, hover .evey-poster the poster or artwork visual (also on the detail page) aspect-ratio, border-radius, shadow, fit .evey-media-detail the media detail page root layout of the detail body theme.css - bigger posters, denser grid, sharper corners
.evey-media-card { width: 12rem; }
.evey-poster     { border-radius: 2px; }
.evey-media-grid { gap: 0.75rem; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)); }
.evey-media-card:hover { transform: scale(1.03); transition: transform 120ms ease; }

docs.title: What the sanitizer rewrites
docs.text:
At install, theme.css goes through a sanitizer that rewrites or removes what a theme may not do, records a warning for each change, and writes the result back: what is served is the sanitized file, which can differ from what you wrote. It never refuses the package.

What you wrote What happens Why @import ... Removed A theme is self-contained; an import is a network leak. url(http://...), url(https://...), url(//...), an external candidate in image-set(), a custom property holding such a URL Replaced with none or neutralized Same reason. data: URIs pass unchanged. url(javascript:...), expression(...), -moz-binding, behavior Removed Legacy execution vectors. A rule whose selector matches [type=password], [type=hidden], .admin-*, .token-* or .secret-* The whole rule block removed A theme must not restyle password fields or privileged elements. A rule with position: fixed or sticky covering the screen: inset: 0, the four sides at 0, or at least two of top/right/bottom/left: 0, width: 100vw, height: 100vh including one viewport size The whole rule block removed The canonical phishing overlay. A header pinned with top: 0; left: 0 and sized by its content is kept. Declarations for the same selector are added up across rules. pointer-events: none in a rule targeting button, [role=button], a[href*=logout] or [data-critical] That declaration removed, the rest kept Hiding clickability on a critical control is a UI redress. z-index above 999 Clamped to 999 A theme stays below the application's own modal layer.

Escaped characters are decoded before these checks, so an escape sequence does not get around them.

docs.title: theme.js
docs.text: A script is optional. It is served at /api/v1/themes/<id>/theme.js to signed-in users and runs in a hidden <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts"> whose policy sets connect-src 'none': no access to the host page, its storage or the network, even for a script that passed the install scan. The only surface is window.evey.theme, injected before the script runs.

docs.title: evey.theme.css(declarations)
docs.text:
Sends custom property declarations to the host page, which applies them on :root. This is the only shape accepted: a --name: value list, up to 200 declarations, each value at most 500 characters, with no url(), image-set, expression(), @import, javascript:, data:, http(s):, //, comment or brace. Anything else is dropped and reported in the console. A property only acts where the sanitized stylesheet references it.

theme.js
evey.theme.css("--accent: #e8a33d; --accent-hover: #f0b95c");

docs.title: evey.theme.log(level, message)
docs.text:
Forwards a line to the browser console. level is "debug", "info", "warn" or "error"; the message is cut at 500 characters. Nothing is shown to the user.

evey.theme.registerComponent and evey.theme.observe exist on the object but are not implemented: the host answers them with an error.

docs.title: What the scanner refuses
docs.text:
At install, theme.js is scanned as text, and a single match refuses the package with the reason. The scanner is deliberately conservative: a theme has no legitimate reason to mention these names, even in a comment.

Any of these substrings, anywhere in the source:

document.cookie, localStorage, sessionStorage, indexedDB, XMLHttpRequest, navigator.sendBeacon, navigator.serviceWorker, WebSocket, EventSource, importScripts, document.write, Element.prototype, Object.defineProperty, globalThis, window.parent, window.top, window.opener, Reflect.get, Reflect.apply, Reflect.construct, window.frames, frameElement, postMessage.

Any of these patterns:

Pattern What it catches \b(fetch\|eval\|atob\|btoa\|Function\|setTimeout\|setInterval)\s*\( Direct calls to forbidden globals \bimport\s*\( Dynamic import (?:window\|self\|globalThis\|top\|parent\|document\|navigator\|location)\s*\[ Bracket access on host globals, such as window["fetch"] \.cookie\b Any .cookie access \.constructor\s*\.\s*constructor The [].constructor.constructor escape new\s+Function\b Code construction (?:window\|self\|top\|parent\|globalThis)\s*\.\s*(?:Function\|eval\|fetch\|atob\|btoa\|XMLHttpRequest\|WebSocket\|EventSource)\b Property read of a forbidden global (?:window\|top\|parent\|document\|location\|globalThis\|self)\s*\.\s*[A-Za-z_$][\w$]*\s*=[^=] Assignment to a host global Object\s*\.\s*prototype Prototype pollution \.register\s*\(\s*['"]\S+\.js Service worker registration

docs.title: Webhooks and API keys
docs.text: Two ways to connect Evey to other tools without writing a plugin: a webhook sends the server's events to a URL of yours, an API key lets a script call the server as you. Both are created by an administrator in the admin panel; this page is for the person who sets them up and for the person who writes the receiver or the script.

docs.title: Send events to a URL
docs.text:
Admin → Webhooks → Create Webhook: a Name, a URL, the Events to send, and an optional Secret for signing. Test sends a ping and reports the answer.

A webhook sending the start and the end of each playback.

Events. A webhook subscribes to All events or to a chosen list. The form offers every event the server publishes; among them:

Area Events Library library.scan.started, library.scan.completed, media.item.added, media.item.updated, media.item.removed, metadata.refreshed Playback playback.started, playback.stopped, media.marked.watched, transcode.started, transcode.failed Accounts user.created, user.login.succeeded, user.login.failed, user.profile.created, user.apikey.created Requests media.request.created, media.request.answered Server backup.created, backup.failed, plugin.installed, plugin.error, server.config.changed

A plugin that calls EmitEvent publishes plugin.event.<type>, which a webhook on All events receives too.

Delivery. Each event is a JSON POST, with two headers:

  • X-Evey-Delivery: an identifier that stays the same across the retries of one delivery, so your receiver can ignore a duplicate;
  • X-Evey-Signature: sha256= followed by the HMAC-SHA256 of the body, computed with the webhook's secret. Verify it with the same secret to know the request comes from your server. Without a secret, the signature proves nothing.

Each attempt waits up to 30 seconds for an answer. A delivery that fails is retried after 1, 5 and 30 seconds. Every attempt is recorded; the history is read through the API (ListWebhookDeliveries in the Plugin API), not in the panel.

Only public addresses

A webhook URL must be http or https and point to a public address. localhost, private and link-local addresses (192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x, 172.16.x.x...), and a name that resolves to one, are refused when the webhook is saved and again when the server connects. This keeps the server from being used to reach your internal network; a receiver on your local network needs a public address or a relay.

docs.title: Call the server from a script
docs.text:
An API key lets a script call the server API without a password. Keys are created in Admin → API Keys → New API Key by an administrator, and belong to that administrator.

  • The key is shown once, when it is created. Store it then; it cannot be displayed again, only revoked with Revoke.
  • It acts as its owner, with administrator rights, within its scopes.
  • Scopes restrict what the key can do:
Scope Allows media:read Reading media metadata media:write Modifying media and starting scans playback:read Reading playback state and history playback:write Controlling playback and progress users:read Reading users users:write Modifying users admin:read Reading administration activity and statistics admin:write Modifying administration settings

A key created without any scope (All (legacy)) has full access on the non-administrative methods, like its owner, but administration methods always require their scope: a legacy key cannot reach them. Select the scopes a script needs.

The key goes in the Authorization header, with or without Bearer:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer evey_..." https://media.example.com/api/v1/...

A key stops working at once when it is revoked, or when its owner is disabled. The endpoints themselves are listed in the Server API, with the other ways to authenticate.

docs.title: Hardware acceleration
docs.text: A graphics card or an integrated GPU lets the server transcode more streams at once, and at higher resolutions, than the processor alone. This page is for the administrator: give the device to the container, leave the panel on Auto, and the server proves on its own what the card can do before it sends a single playback to it.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
1. Open Admin → Transcoding → Encode calibration. Hardware acceleration is on Auto (best available) by default, and the Detected: line names the accelerators the host advertises.
  2. If it says No GPU accelerator detected, give the device to the container (next section) and recreate it.
  3. Click Recalibrate, or wait: the server measures itself at its first quiet moment. The card then shows the backend in use and the resolutions certified for the GPU and for the processor.

There is one image for every case: no driver is baked in for a specific card, and the same container runs in software only, with an Intel or AMD GPU, or with an NVIDIA card, depending on the devices you give it.

docs.title: Give the device to the container
docs.text:
Intel / AMD (VAAPI, Quick Sync)NVIDIA (NVENC)Rockchip (RKMPP) docker-compose.yml
services:
  evey:
    devices:
      - /dev/dri:/dev/dri
    group_add:
      - "104"   # the host's render group: getent group render

The group must be the host's render group (getent group render, or stat -c %g /dev/dri/renderD128). A wrong value does not break anything: the GPU is simply not accessible and the server stays on the processor.

Install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit on the host, then reserve the GPU and request the video capability, without which the encoder library is not injected:

docker-compose.yml
services:
  evey:
    environment:
      NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES: all   # must include "video"
    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: all
              capabilities: [gpu]

Map /dev/mpp_service, /dev/dri and, where the kernel exposes it, /dev/rga. See ARM hosts.

Both an NVIDIA reservation and /dev/dri can be mapped at once.

docs.title: What "proved by a real encode" means
docs.text:
With Auto, the server works only from measurements, never from the name of the card:

  1. Detect. Each render node is probed for VAAPI and, on Intel, Quick Sync; each NVIDIA GPU and the Rockchip encoder likewise. An encoder counts only if a short real encode through it succeeds.
  2. Certify. Each accelerator encodes the resolution ladder (720p to 2160p) in the same pipeline shape as real playback and keeps the highest rung it sustains at 1.2 times real time. A few frames of each probe are decoded back and compared with the source, because a faulty driver can exit cleanly while producing green or garbled frames. An accelerator that cannot sustain 720p is not used.
  3. Measure the routes. For each capability the accelerator proved (SDR, HEVC, AV1, tone mapping on the GPU, HDR kept), the cost of a real session is measured.
  4. Choose per stream. Each playback goes to the cheapest accelerator that has proved what that stream needs, or to the processor. See Transcoding and server capacity.

The measurement waits for a quiet moment: no active stream and the host's CPU under 20 % for five samples in a row, four seconds apart, so that a busy boot or a library scan does not pin the ceilings too low. It runs again when the hardware changes. Recalibrate runs it immediately: use it after adding a card or moving the container to another machine.

A cold boot is not a verdict

A GPU that fails to initialise in the first seconds after the container starts is probed again on a short schedule before anything is recorded. Only a failure that stays, or one of a deterministic kind (missing encoder, unsupported format), marks the accelerator as unusable.

docs.title: Forcing a backend or turning it off
docs.text:
Off (software only) keeps every transcode on the processor, which is the escape hatch for a faulty driver. Choosing a Backend by hand (NVENC, VAAPI, QSV, RKMPP) forces that one; if it turns out unusable, the server falls back to the processor and the card shows the backend actually in use.

On a machine with several accelerators, Auto has no fixed preference: each is certified and measured, and every stream goes to the backend that proved the route it needs, at the best proven quality and the lowest measured cost. Two streams on the same server can therefore use different backends, for example HDR tone mapping on one card and an HEVC encode on another.

docs.title: Checking that it is used
docs.text:
Admin → Transcoding → Encode calibration shows the accelerators detected, the backend in use, the resolutions certified for the GPU and for the processor, and under Hardware fallbacks the recent encodes that fell back to the processor with their cause. During playback, Admin → Now Playing names the backend each stream is encoded with.

Under WSL2, NVENC works; VAAPI and Quick Sync do not (the WSL graphics driver fails on these encodes), and the panel marks them not supported on WSL.

docs.title: Libraries and metadata
docs.text:
A library is a type and a set of folders: Evey walks the folders, recognises each file from its name and fetches its details (titles, summaries, posters, cast, ratings). This page is for the administrator who adds one: the three things you will do first (add a library, name the files, fix a wrong match) come first; how scans run, music and photo specifics, collections and the metadata sources follow.

Admin → Libraries: one row per library, with its folders, its item count and its last scan.

docs.title: Add a library
docs.text:
1. Admin → Libraries → Add Library.
  2. Give it a Name and a Type. Keep films and series in separate libraries: the type tells the scanner what to look for.
  3. Under Paths, pick a folder from the list, or Enter custom path... to type one; + Add Path adds a second folder to the same library.
  4. Create Library. The first walk of the folders follows within a couple of minutes; Scan on the row starts it right away. Posters and summaries arrive in the background, so a large library fills in over a few minutes.
Type Recognised as Metadata from Movies One film per file (or per folder) TMDB, completed by OMDb when a key is set TV Shows Series, seasons, episodes TMDB Music Artists, albums, tracks The files' tags; covers from the files, the album folder, Cover Art Archive (MusicBrainz), then iTunes Photos Albums, pictures with their shooting details The files

Paths are the container's

The folder picker lists what the container sees. With the installation's compose file, your media folder is /media, so a folder /srv/media/films on the host is /media/films for Evey. A second mounted folder (/media2) is added the same way.

docs.title: Name files so they are recognised
docs.text:
The scanner recognises names like these:

/media/films/The Mirror (1999)/The Mirror (1999) 1080p.mkv
/media/films/Lantern.2010.1080p.BluRay.x264.mkv
/media/series/The Outpost/Season 01/The.Outpost.S01E05.720p.mkv
/media/series/Quiet Storm/Quiet.Storm.03x10.mkv

For a film, the year matters most. For an episode, S01E05 or 1x05. Release tags (resolution, source, codec, audio, language tags such as VOSTFR or MULTI, editions such as "Director's Cut") are removed before the search.

If your files carry a tag the parser does not know, add it in Admin → Server Config → Parser tokens: Extra quality tokens for single words (HDRIP), Extra edition suffixes for phrases. It applies from the next scan.

docs.title: Fix a wrong or missing title
docs.text:
For one title, open it and choose Edit Metadata:

  • Identify on TMDB searches TMDB by title; Use this match applies the result. This is the quickest fix for a film matched to a namesake.
  • The fields change the details by hand. A value you edit is kept: later refreshes do not overwrite it. Changing TMDB ID or IMDB ID fetches the details of that id when you save.
  • Refresh metadata fetches the details again for the current match. Reset metadata and Re-match metadata start over from the file name, dropping your edits; Reset also wipes artwork and cast, and the seasons and episodes of a series.

For a whole library, the row in Admin → Libraries offers:

  • Match orphans only retries the files that were never recognised. It is fast.
  • Re-match all from TMDB redoes the search for every title. It is slow, and corrects old mistakes after a large renaming.
  • Repair sagas joins films that belong to no collection back to their saga, when the other films of the saga are already in the library.

docs.title: How new files are picked up
docs.text:
The server walks every library at each start, then every 2 minutes (Admin → Server Config → Server Settings → Periodic scan interval, applied on restart). While something is playing, the walks are spaced out to 15 minutes so they do not compete with playback for the disk. A new, renamed or deleted file is therefore seen within minutes without any setting.

Two more ways to scan, on the library's row:

Action Effect Scan A walk now. The row shows Scanning... then the result; a folder that could not be read is named. Schedule A full scan Every 6 hours, Every 12 hours, Daily (3 AM), Weekly (Sunday 3 AM), or on a Cron expression.

The server also watches folders for file system events (Admin → Server Config → Server Settings → Library file watcher), on the libraries whose realtime monitoring is on. It checks that the watch still answers by writing a probe file into the folder for a few seconds; a library whose watch is proven alive is walked once an hour instead of every 2 minutes, the others keep the periodic walk. Libraries created from the panel are not watched: the periodic walk is what picks their files up.

Network shares

On an NFS or SMB share, a file written by another machine raises no event on the server. The periodic walk is what finds it.

docs.title: Music libraries
docs.text:
The scanner reads MP3, FLAC, M4A, OGG, Opus, WAV and AAC files, and takes each track from its tags: title (the file name when it is missing), artist, album artist, album, year, track and disc numbers, genre. Artists are grouped by album artist, or by artist when that tag is empty.

An album is a folder. Tracks are grouped by the folder they sit in, not by their album tag: two folders sharing one album tag are two albums, and an album split into CD1 and CD2 subfolders shows as two. Keep each album in one folder; its tracks are ordered by disc number, then track number, and the album takes the name most of its tracks carry.

The cover is the picture embedded in the files, otherwise an image in the album folder (cover.jpg, folder.jpg or front.jpg), otherwise Cover Art Archive (found through MusicBrainz), otherwise iTunes.

docs.title: Photo libraries
docs.text: The scanner reads JPEG, PNG, HEIC, WebP, GIF, TIFF and BMP files. A photo's album is its folder, relative to the library folder; a photo at the top level has none, and moving a file to another folder moves it to that album at the next scan. The date taken and the camera model come from the EXIF data of JPEG files; the other formats are listed without them. Thumbnails are resized on the server and kept in the transcoding cache.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
Collections gathers titles under one name, for every account. There are three kinds:

  • TMDB Collections: the sagas, filled in on their own when TMDB places a film in one. Repair sagas (above) catches films that missed theirs.
  • New collection: a list an administrator fills by hand, with Add to collection on a title or on a selection, and puts in order.
  • New smart collection: rules on Genre, Year, Type, Rating ≥ and Library, which a title must all meet. Its content is worked out each time it is opened, so new titles appear without doing anything.

Only administrators create and edit collections. Anyone can browse them, and Download collection on the web gets the original files as one ZIP (up to 1000 titles), leaving out what the account's library access or age limit hides.

docs.title: Metadata keys
docs.text:
Evey ships with a TMDB key, so metadata works without configuration. Other sources are optional; their keys go in Admin → Server Config → API Keys, and a key set there wins over the same key given in the environment (see Environment: libraries and metadata).

Key Adds TMDB (your own) Your own request quota instead of the shared one. OMDb A second source for films TMDB knows little about. OpenSubtitles Searching and downloading subtitles a file does not carry, through the server API (the apps do not offer it yet). See Subtitles. TheIntroDB Intro, recap and credits timings from a community database: 500 lookups a day with a key instead of 100 without.

docs.title: Intro, recap and credits
docs.text:
Evey marks the intro, the recap and the credits of episodes and films so the players can offer to skip them. The timings come from community databases (TheIntroDB, then IntroDB) when they know the title, and from the server's own analysis of the files otherwise. An administrator can adjust the segments of a title by hand, or run the detection again.

Players show Skip Intro, Skip Recap and Skip Credits buttons by default. Auto-skip intros (Admin → Server Config → Server Settings, off by default) makes every player skip them on its own.

docs.title: Remote access and HTTPS
docs.text: Publish the server at an https:// address and the people in your household can use it from anywhere. This page is for the administrator: it covers the public address, the remote-access switch the server sets on its own, and what Evey needs to know about the reverse proxy in front of it.

docs.title: Publish the server in three steps
docs.text:
1. Put a reverse proxy in front of Evey that terminates HTTPS and forwards everything to port 9091: the bundled Caddy, or a proxy you already run. Ready-made configurations are in Reverse proxy configurations.
  2. In Admin → Remote Access, set External URL to the https:// address and, when the proxy runs in another container, its network in Trusted proxies (172.16.0.0/12 for Docker's default networks).
  3. Nothing else: a server given a public address opens remote access on its own. evey admin doctor confirms the proxy list in force and warns when a published server is refusing remote clients.

docs.title: Remote access is decided from the public address
docs.text:
Evey decides remote access at startup unless you have chosen it yourself:

  • if the server was given a public address (External URL, EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL or EVEY_REMOTE_ACCESS_EXTERNAL_URL), remote access is on;
  • otherwise it is off, and only clients on your local networks are served.

Once you change Enable Remote Access yourself, your choice is kept and the server no longer infers it: a published server can stay LAN-only if that is what you want. Remote access is a choice about who may reach the server, not a protection: every page still requires signing in.

When remote access is off, a client outside the local networks receives a 403 on every page, and the apps show a message saying remote access is disabled rather than a generic error. If the server is reachable from the internet while remote access is off, the admin page shows Every remote user is locked out, the server logs it at startup and logs each refusal with the client address, and evey admin doctor reports it as a failure.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Admin → Remote Access. Every setting applies without a restart: the network ones to the next request, the bitrate to the next playback.

A server published at an https:// address behind a proxy on the Docker network. Setting Effect Enable Remote Access On: clients outside the local networks are served like any other. Off: they get a 403. External URL The public address. E-mail links, single sign-on redirects and cast URLs are built from it. An https:// address also turns on HTTPS mode (below). Trusted proxies The reverse proxies whose forwarded client address Evey believes. Loopback is always trusted. Empty: the list comes from EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES. LAN Networks The address ranges treated as home. Private ranges are listed by default. Add a VPN range (Tailscale, WireGuard) here if its clients should count as home. Max Remote Bitrate A bitrate ceiling for clients outside the local networks, in kbit/s (0 = none). A private address is never capped. When Admin → Transcoding also sets a ceiling for remote viewers, the lower of the two applies. See How playback is decided.

docs.title: What Evey needs to know about the proxy
docs.text:
Evey serves plain HTTP on port 9091, API and web interface together. HTTPS is the job of the reverse proxy, and Evey needs two things about it, both in Admin → Remote Access:

  • External URL in https://. This is what tells Evey a proxy terminates TLS: cookies get the Secure flag, HSTS is sent and the X-Forwarded-Proto header of a trusted proxy is believed.
  • Trusted proxies, when the proxy is not on the same machine as Evey. A proxy in another container needs its network here, for example 172.16.0.0/12 for Docker's default networks.

A range covering every address is refused

0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 in Trusted proxies would let any client choose the address it is seen with. The panel and evey admin doctor both refuse it: list the proxy's own address or network.

docs.title: Setting it in the environment instead
docs.text: EVEY_SERVER_BASE_URL and EVEY_TRUSTED_PROXIES give the same answers from the compose file, which suits an installation described entirely as code or a server that must be reachable over HTTPS from its very first start. The panel wins when both are set: an https:// External URL enables HTTPS mode even if the base URL is plain HTTP, and a saved proxy list replaces the variable. Emptying the field hands the answer back to the variable. See Server and network.

docs.title: The real client address
docs.text:
Remote access and Max Remote Bitrate both depend on Evey seeing each client's real address, in two successive steps: the trusted proxies decide whose forwarded address is believed, and so which address each client gets; the LAN networks then classify that address as local or remote.

A proxy that does not forward the address, or that Evey does not trust, makes every request look like it comes from the proxy's private address: everyone counts as home, the remote-access setting has no effect and no remote cap applies.

Fixing the proxy changes who counts as remote

If remote access was off, remote clients are refused from the moment the proxy forwards their real address. Check evey admin doctor after changing proxy settings: it names the list in force and where it comes from, warns about a public range and fails on a range covering every address.

docs.title: Users, profiles and parental control
docs.text: An account signs in; a profile watches. This page is for the administrator who adds the household: create the accounts, let each one create its profiles, mark the children's profiles as kids profiles and give them an age limit. What an account can be restricted to, opening hours, requests, public download links and the home page come after.

docs.title: Accounts and profiles
docs.text: An account has a username and a password (or a single sign-on identity, see OIDC), and it is either an administrator or not. Each account holds one or more profiles, each with its own watch history, resume points, favourites, languages and home page. A household typically shares one account, with a profile per person.

docs.title: Create an account
docs.text:
Admin → Users: each account with its profiles, its role and its state.

Admin → Users offers two ways:

  • Create User: you choose the Username and the Password, tick Admin for an administrator, and can set the libraries, the number of profiles and the number of devices right there (see below).
  • Create Invite Link: the person chooses their own. A link can have an expiry date (Expires at) and a maximum number of uses (Max uses), restrict the libraries the new account sees (Accessible libraries), cap the number of profiles it may create, and Create as administrator. Invite Links lists them; Copy Link copies one, Revoke ends it.

Disable on an account's row refuses its sign-ins without deleting anything; Enable restores it. Delete removes the account and its profiles.

docs.title: Profiles, kids profiles and the PIN
docs.text:
Each account creates its profiles in Settings → Profiles → Create Profile; an administrator can also add one from Edit User → New profile. A profile has a Name, a Language and a Region, and two settings that matter for children:

  • Kids profile marks the profile as a child's. It opens without a PIN, and leaving it for another profile asks for that profile's PIN (4 digits). While a kids profile exists, every other profile of the account must have a PIN: the server refuses to save a profile without one. Setting a PIN the first time asks for the account password; changing it asks for the current PIN. Settings → Parental sets the PIN of the profile in use.
