Browsers that decode Dolby Digital natively, such as Safari, receive it as an ordinary track; the choice is made by testing the browser, not by recognising it. A surround track is decoded in the page only when the profile's Max Audio Channels allows it: a profile set to stereo gets the AAC re-encode instead, which can fold the channels.

Warning

A reverse proxy that sets its own Content-Security-Policy must allow 'wasm-unsafe-eval' in script-src, otherwise the decoder cannot start and the film plays without sound. See Reverse proxy configurations.

docs.title: Sound out of sync
docs.text:
Audio sync in the player shifts the sound for the current title (positive values play it later). It is offered when the stream comes from the server as a remux or a transcode; in Direct Play the control reads Available during transcoded playback only. Applying a shift restarts the stream at the current position. A copied track cannot be shifted, so the server re-encodes it and Stream info shows Audio resync requested.

When the offset is in the file itself (an audio track that starts after the picture, or tracks that disagree with each other), Admin → Media Health reports it but never rewrites it on its own: an offset that starts late is usually a deliberate dub alignment. Check sync on the file's row lets you judge it by eye and apply a shift, which its history can undo. See Media health.

docs.title: Casting
docs.text: What the television plays when you cast, and why it can differ from what your phone or browser was playing. For viewers using the Cast button of the web player in Chrome or of the Android app, towards a Chromecast or a TV with Chromecast built in; the Android TV app has no Cast button. The phone or the browser only starts the session: the TV plays the stream from the server directly, through Evey's own receiver application, and the server decides what to send for the TV, not for the device that cast.

docs.title: What the TV plays
docs.text:
The stream is decoded by the TV, so the playback decision uses the receiver's capabilities, from the most reliable source available:

  1. What the receiver observed on itself. Evey's receiver tests its own device when it starts (which codecs and resolutions it can display, whether it displays HDR, whether it passes Dolby audio through, how many audio channels its output carries) and reports it. When this report arrives, it is the one used.
  2. Otherwise, the model. The name the Cast SDK reports (Chromecast with Google TV, Chromecast Ultra, Google TV Streamer...) maps to the documented capabilities of that family.
  3. Otherwise, a conservative profile. An unknown device, a receiver that did not answer in time, or a device found without a model name gets the capabilities of the oldest Chromecast: H.264 up to 1080p, SDR, no Dolby.

The order follows the cost of a mistake: assuming a capability the device does not have gives a black screen, while assuming too little only costs a transcode. In practice: HDR reaches the TV only when its receiver reported an HDR screen; Dolby Digital (AC-3, E-AC-3) is sent as it is only to a receiver that reported passing it through natively, otherwise it is re-encoded to AAC. A receiver that claimed surround and then failed to load the stream reloads once with a stereo ceiling.

docs.title: When the TV's connection is slow
docs.text:
Before asking for a stream, the receiver measures its own throughput and sends it with the request. The server keeps the original video when that throughput carries it with a 20 % margin. Otherwise it chooses the highest quality the connection carries. If playback stalls anyway, the receiver reloads once on the lowest quality, provided that halves the bitrate. Stream info then shows The line the client measured cannot carry the copy or Survival rung asked for by the player.

Older cast devices do not switch quality on their own during playback; this is why the server makes that choice for them.

docs.title: Browsers without a Cast session of their own
docs.text:
In the web player the Cast button appears when the browser can cast: Chrome on a computer, which opens its Google Cast picker, and browsers that support remote playback, such as Safari or Chrome on Android. Firefox shows none.

Where the browser cannot open a Cast session itself (Safari, Chrome on Android), a tap goes through the server, which tries in this order and takes the first device it finds at each step:

  1. a Chromecast on the network of the device you are holding, played through Evey's receiver as above;
  2. a DLNA TV on the server's network. It receives the stream the browser was playing (the original file in Direct Play, the transcoded stream otherwise): no decision is made for the TV itself;
  3. your own Evey apps open and signed in to the same account: a single one takes the film over, as with Play on; with several, the player points to Play on to choose;
  4. the browser's own device picker.

Note

Steps 1 and 2 pick the first device found, not one you choose. With several Chromecasts at home, cast from Chrome on a computer or from the Android app, which both show a picker.

docs.title: When a cast does not work
docs.text: A cast froze, went silent, or the phone keeps spinning.

docs.title: HDR and Dolby Vision
docs.text: What an HDR or Dolby Vision title looks like on your screen, and why: the original picture, a re-encode that keeps the HDR, or an SDR conversion. For viewers who wonder why a film looks different from one device to another, and for admins sizing a server. The general rules of playback are in How playback is decided.

docs.title: What you will see, by device
docs.text:
Your screen What arrives An HDR screen on Android TV or an Android phone, with an HEVC decoder The HDR10 or HLG original, untouched, unless something else (bitrate, resolution, a burned-in subtitle) forces a re-encode. A browser An SDR conversion, always: the web player does not declare an HDR screen, so the server tone-maps for it. A cast receiver What the receiver reported about its own screen: see Casting. An SDR screen, anywhere An SDR conversion.

Showing HDR on an SDR screen without conversion gives washed-out, grey colours, so the server never sends it. The Android apps probe the display at each playback start, not once at install: plugging an HDR television into a box takes effect at the next title, track switch or quality change.

docs.title: When the original is kept
docs.text: The HDR10 or HLG video is sent as it is when the player reports that its screen displays HDR and it decodes the codec, and no other reason (bitrate, resolution, container) requires a re-encode.

docs.title: When the video must be re-encoded anyway
docs.text:
A bitrate limit, a resolution limit or a subtitle to burn in can force a re-encode of an HDR source. The HDR is then kept if all of these hold:

  • the player reports an HDR screen and decodes HEVC;
  • the server has a graphics card that proved, during its measurement, that it encodes HEVC 10-bit with HDR;
  • that card is available for this stream.

The result is HEVC 10-bit with the source's HDR signalling (BT.2020 colour, PQ or HLG transfer) carried over. HDR10+ dynamic metadata is not carried: an HDR10+ title plays as HDR10 on this path.

When one of the conditions fails, the processor or the card tone-maps the picture to SDR before encoding it. Stream info then lists HDR converted to SDR (tone-mapping).

If the original could have been sent but the server cannot serve it as a copy yet (its seek index is still being built, for example), the video is re-encoded with the HDR kept on such a card, and Stream info shows Copy unavailable, HDR kept through the re-encode.

docs.title: When the screen is SDR
docs.text:
A player that does not report an HDR screen receives a tone-mapped SDR picture. Tone mapping runs on the graphics card when it has proved it can (VAAPI with OpenCL, for example), otherwise on the processor: with a SIMD-optimised filter (AVX2) when the ffmpeg build provides it, with a portable filter chain otherwise.

Note

On the processor, tone mapping is the most expensive transcode there is. The server measures a separate, usually lower, resolution ceiling for HDR, so an HDR title may be converted at a lower resolution than an SDR one on the same machine. See Transcoding.

docs.title: Dolby Vision
docs.text:
A player's report says whether its screen displays HDR, not whether it supports Dolby Vision, and Evey never infers Dolby Vision support from HDR support: sending Dolby Vision to a screen that only handles HDR10 gives wrong colours. The stream is copied only when it carries a base layer that displays correctly without any Dolby Vision decoding:

Dolby Vision profile HDR player SDR player 8.1 (HDR10-compatible base layer) Treated as HDR10: the rules above apply, the original can be kept. Tone-mapped to SDR. 7 (UHD Blu-ray) The HDR10 base layer is re-encoded as HEVC 10-bit with HDR kept. Stream info: Dolby Vision base layer re-encoded (HDR kept). Tone-mapped to SDR. 5 (no HDR10 base layer) Tone-mapped to SDR. Tone-mapped to SDR.

docs.title: Checking what happened
docs.text: Stream info shows the video decision and, among the reasons, the tone mapping or the HDR kept. Every route that tone-maps reports it there, with one exception: when the graphics card is full at the moment a stream starts, the stream moves to the processor after Stream info was computed. Admin → Now Playing shows the backend actually used.

docs.title: How playback is decided
docs.text:
Why does this film play untouched on the TV and get re-encoded on the phone? This page answers that for anyone who presses play: the three outcomes and how to read Stream info come first; the exact rules the server applies follow, for the reader who wants to understand or tune them.

Evey never asks you to pick a quality before playing. Each start of a title is a negotiation between three parties: what the file contains, what this player can decode, and what this server can encode right now. The same film can therefore be sent as it is to one device and re-encoded for another, or play differently on the same device when the server is busy.

docs.title: The three outcomes
docs.text:
In Stream info What the player receives What it costs the server Direct Play The original file, byte for byte. A file read. Remux The original video and audio in another container. Nothing is re-encoded. Repackaging, done by MKVGo inside the server where it can, by an FFmpeg copy otherwise. Transcode At least one track re-encoded. Often only the audio, with the video still the original. An encode. Only a video re-encode takes a transcoding slot.

The server tries them in that order, and within a transcode it re-encodes only the tracks that need it.

docs.title: Reading Stream info
docs.text:
Stream info (the information button, (i), in the player's controls; on the TV, in the player's options menu) shows the Method, then each track with its decision (copied, transcoded, or client-decoded for audio the web player decodes itself), and under Why not direct play the reasons.

Remux: the packaging changes, the video and audio tracks are left intact, and the one reason the file is not played as it is. "Copied" describes the tracks, not the playback method.

The reasons fall into four groups:

Where the reason comes from Examples as shown The player cannot use the track as it is Video codec this player cannot decode · Audio codec this player cannot decode · Resolution above the player's limit · More audio channels than this player supports · Pixel format the player cannot decode (10-bit H.264, 4:2:2) · Container not playable as-is (repackaged to HLS) A limit on this session Bitrate above the allowed limit · The line the client measured cannot carry the copy A consequence for the picture or the sound HDR converted to SDR (tone-mapping) · Subtitles burned into the picture · Audio resync requested A setting or a decision already taken Direct Play turned off in the profile · Remux turned off in the profile · Preferred video codec (profile setting) · Choice pinned for this session

Only the audio track being played is judged. A file whose unselected commentary track is in DTS is not transcoded because of it.

Stream info is computed when playback starts. The one case it cannot foresee is a graphics card that is full at the moment the stream starts: the stream then moves to the processor, and Admin → Now Playing shows the backend actually used.

docs.title: What each side brings
docs.text:
The file. Codec, resolution, bit depth, HDR format, bitrate, and the audio and subtitle tracks, read when the file was scanned.

The player. When playback starts, the app reports what its device can decode: the codec families it supports, the containers it opens, its maximum resolution, whether its screen displays HDR, how many audio channels it outputs, and for some devices a lower ceiling or level for H.264. The web app asks the browser; the Android and Android TV apps ask the device's decoders and display. Evey keeps no list of supported devices: it uses what the player reports. A cast session is described by the receiver itself when it can report its capabilities, and by a conservative profile otherwise: see Casting.

The session. The profile's preferences (maximum bitrate, maximum audio channels, subtitle handling) and the limits that apply to this viewer, below.

The server. Whether it can encode this in real time, on its graphics card or its processor, and whether a transcoding slot is free. This is measured, not assumed: see Transcoding and server capacity.

docs.title: One file, three results
docs.text:
A 4K HEVC film in HDR10 at 70 Mb/s, with a Dolby TrueHD 7.1 track, played on an Android TV whose decoder handles HEVC and whose screen displays HDR:

  • No bitrate limit. The TV decodes the video and displays the HDR, so the video is kept as it is. It does not decode TrueHD, so only the audio is re-encoded. Stream info shows Transcode, with the video copied.
  • A limit of 20 Mb/s, and a graphics card that encodes HEVC 10-bit with HDR. The video must be re-encoded to fit. The server re-encodes it in HEVC and keeps the HDR, because both the TV and the card can.
  • The same limit, with the graphics card busy or unavailable for this title. The processor takes over. It encodes H.264, which carries no HDR here, so the picture is tone-mapped to SDR, at the quality the processor sustains.

The file and the TV did not change. The session limit and the server's state did.

docs.title: Limits on the session
docs.text:
A title whose bitrate (video plus the audio track being played) is above the lowest of these limits is transcoded down to it:

  • the maximum the player reports;
  • the account's Max Bitrate, set by an administrator;
  • the profile's Max Streaming Bitrate, and its Max Cellular Bitrate when a phone reports a mobile connection;
  • Max Remote Bitrate (Admin → Remote Access) and Video bitrate ceiling, remote viewers (Admin → Transcoding), the lower of the two, when the viewer's address is public and outside the LAN Networks. A private address is never capped.

The audio track being played is re-encoded when it has more channels than the player reports or than the profile's Max Audio Channels. A re-encoded track keeps up to 5.1 channels, never more: see Audio.

docs.title: Constraints the server applies itself
docs.text: A few limits are not reported by players today and are applied by the server as a conservative compatibility rule, the same for every player: 10-bit H.264, and any video in 4:2:2, 4:4:4 or 12-bit, are re-encoded, while HEVC, VP9 and AV1 up to 10-bit 4:2:0 are left to the player's codec support. Dolby Vision is kept only in a form the player can display correctly: see HDR and Dolby Vision.

docs.title: Why the method rarely changes mid-film
docs.text: The decision is taken when playback starts and kept for the session, so the player never receives segments from two different encodings. Changing the audio or subtitle track in a way that needs it, or restarting the title, takes a new decision.

docs.title: Forcing a method
docs.text:
Settings → Playback has Allow direct play, Allow remux and Allow transcoding per profile. Turning one off makes the server skip that method, and Stream info shows why.

Note

This is a diagnostic tool, not a quality setting: a forced transcode is never better than the original.

Quality, in the player's settings, is different: it chooses among the qualities of a transcoded stream. Auto follows the connection; a height (1080p, 720p...) holds that quality; Original removes the height limit the player would otherwise ask for.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Criteria in detail: HDR and Dolby Vision · Audio · Subtitles · Casting
  • How the server shares its capacity: Transcoding and server capacity
  • What runs inside the server without FFmpeg: MKVGo in Evey
  • The implementation: Playback pipeline

docs.title: MKVGo in Evey
docs.text:
MKVGo is the media library Evey runs inside its own process to read and repackage MKV/WebM and MP4/MOV files. This page is for the reader who wants to know what the server does without starting FFmpeg, and where FFmpeg still takes over.

MKVGo works on the structure of a file: its headers, its index, its tracks and their packets. It never decodes or encodes a picture or a sound; everything that needs server-side decoding goes to FFmpeg. It is developed as a separate Go library: github.com/gravity-zero/mkvgo.

docs.title: Three levels of work
docs.text:
Level What happens What it costs the server Direct Play The file is served as it is. A file read. MKVGo Structural work: reading a file, repackaging its tracks for streaming, rebuilding its index, moving a track on the timeline. Code inside the server process: no FFmpeg or ffprobe started per stream, and no segments written to disk for on-demand packaging. FFmpeg Real transformations: re-encoding, tone mapping, decoding a picture. Also the fallback whenever MKVGo cannot handle a file. One process per job.

An FFmpeg copy (-c copy) re-encodes nothing either and stays cheap; what MKVGo saves on top is the process started for each session and the segments written to the transcoding cache. A re-encode is the expensive case, and a video re-encode is the only work that takes a transcoding slot: see Transcoding and server capacity.

On capable clients, around 80% of video playback paths can avoid FFmpeg entirely: what the player decodes decides how often the file can be served as it is or only repackaged. How that is decided: How playback is decided.

docs.title: What MKVGo does
docs.text: Work Where it shows When MKVGo cannot Reading files During a library scan, codecs, resolution, HDR, bitrate and duration are read from the head of the file. ffprobe reads it. It also takes over on any doubt: a parse error, or colour information MKVGo could not read on an HDR-capable codec. Keyframe index The positions playback can start from, read from the file's index; they let Remux and video copy cut segments on keyframes. ffprobe. Streaming without re-encoding Remux: HLS segments in fragmented MP4 (CMAF), built on request from a plan kept per file. A DASH manifest is produced over the same segments; the apps use HLS. FFmpeg copies the tracks, still without re-encoding. MP4 for the browser A Matroska file a browser cannot open is rewritten once as a fast-start MP4, kept in a cache. - Subtitles Subtitle tracks embedded in an MKV are extracted to SRT or ASS. - Preview images The keyframe nearest the requested position is found through the index, and FFmpeg decodes only that frame. Used when that keyframe is within about two seconds of the request. FFmpeg seeks and decodes up to the exact position. Episode chains The server can package several episodes as one continuous stream (?gapless=1 on the stream address). No app offers the switch yet. Each episode plays on its own. Media Health The diagnosis (seek index, audio start, tracks stored in blocks), the rebuilt index, the resync past a damaged stretch, and moving an audio track by an offset. See Media health. Re-muxing tracks stored in blocks is done by FFmpeg.

docs.title: What stays with FFmpeg
docs.text:
• Every re-encode, including HDR tone mapping.
  • Decoding pictures: the seek bar thumbnails, the frame of a preview image.
  • Analysis that needs decoded data: interlace detection, audio fingerprints for intro detection.
  • Containers other than MKV/WebM and MP4/MOV, such as AVI or MPEG-TS.

docs.title: Seeing which engine served a stream
docs.text: Admin → Dashboard and Admin → Now Playing name the engine of each track: mkvgo or ffmpeg. A Remux can show both, for example the video packaged by MKVGo and the audio copied by FFmpeg.

docs.title: Subtitles
docs.text: How a subtitle is shown on your device, and whether choosing it changes how the video is delivered. For viewers; the only setting that matters is the profile's Subtitle Burn-in, in Settings → Playback. The short answer: text and Blu-ray subtitles never touch the video, DVD and broadcast subtitles are burned in and force a re-encode.

docs.title: What each format does to the video
docs.text:
Format Examples How it is shown Effect on the video Text SRT, ASS/SSA, WebVTT, subtitles inside the file Sent alongside the video and drawn by the player, with your Subtitle Style None PGS (Blu-ray) hdmv_pgs_subtitle Decoded into images once by the server, cached, and drawn by the player as they are None Other picture formats VobSub (DVD), DVB, XSUB Burned into the picture by the server The video is re-encoded

Every player (web, Android, Android TV) draws text and PGS subtitles itself, so choosing one never changes how the video is delivered. Only the last row does: burning subtitles into the picture requires decoding and re-encoding the video, so a title that played directly becomes a transcode. Stream info then lists Subtitles burned into the picture.

A picture subtitle is burned in only when you actually select it. A file that merely carries one, or marks it as default, keeps its Direct Play.

docs.title: Subtitle Burn-in
docs.text:
The profile setting Subtitle Burn-in (Settings → Playback) governs the formats of the last row:

Setting A selected VobSub, DVB or XSUB track Text and PGS Auto Burned in, the video is re-encoded. Drawn by the player. Always burn in Same as Auto. Drawn by the player: text is never burned in, whatever the setting. Never burn in Cannot be shown: the video is never re-encoded for a subtitle. Drawn by the player.

docs.title: Choosing and adjusting
docs.text:
• The players select the subtitle of the profile's Default Subtitle Language, then the track the file marks as default (a forced track, for example). A track chosen by hand is never overridden, and a new title starts the choice from scratch.
  • Subtitle sync in the player shifts the subtitles for the current title (positive values show them later). It applies at once.
  • Subtitle Style sets the size, text colour, background, font, shadow and position of text subtitles. PGS images are drawn as they are.
  • Upload subtitle… adds a file for the title.
  • With an OpenSubtitles key (see Libraries and metadata), the server API can search for and download a subtitle the file does not carry (GET /api/v1/media/{id}/subtitles/search, then POST /api/v1/media/{id}/subtitles/download). The file is saved in a .subtitles folder next to the film. The apps do not offer this search.

docs.title: Transcoding and server capacity
docs.text: Transcoding is the expensive outcome of the playback decision: Direct Play and Remux cost the server almost nothing and never take a transcoding slot. This page is for the administrator who wants to know how many viewers the server can serve at once: how it measures what it can encode, how it shares that capacity, and what a viewer sees when it is full.

docs.title: The server measures itself
docs.text:
The capacity is not a setting you estimate. The server measures it:

  • When. Not at startup: the server starts on what it knew before (or on a conservative 720p software default the first time), and runs the measurement at its first quiet moment, when nobody is watching and the processor is mostly idle. It takes a few minutes. A measurement taken under load is marked provisional and redone when the machine is idle.
  • What. Real encodes of a 4K clip, in SDR and in HDR, on the processor and on each accelerator the server detected, in the same shape as a real playback. The result is the highest resolution each one sustains in real time, and the cost of each kind of stream.
  • Again. After the hardware changes, or on Recalibrate in Admin → Transcoding → Encode calibration. The button waits until nobody is watching.

While the measurement runs, a playback that needs a transcode shows The server is calibrating itself and is asked to try again shortly. Direct Play and Remux are not affected.

On a processor that sustains none of the resolutions, the server still offers 720p (SDR) and 480p (HDR), one stream at a time.

The measurement uses, in this order, a clip you provide, a reference clip downloaded once and checked by its SHA256, or a synthetic clip generated on the spot. A real clip measures more honestly than the synthetic one, which overstates the cost and can cap a machine lower than it deserves:

docker-compose.yml
services:
  evey:
    environment:
      EVEY_BENCH_HDR_SAMPLE: /data/bench/my-4k-hdr.hevc
      EVEY_BENCH_SDR_SAMPLE: /data/bench/my-4k-sdr.hevc

docs.title: Sharing the capacity
docs.text:
Live playback capacity (Admin → Transcoding) is the number of video streams that may be encoded at the same time. It is derived from the measurement and adjusts on its own when the hardware changes. Limit simultaneous video streams can lower it, never raise it.

  • A transcode that only re-encodes the audio (video copied) uses no slot.
  • A viewer changing quality keeps a single slot.
  • Only the quality a viewer actually watches is encoded, not the whole ladder of qualities.

Each stream goes to the cheapest route that has proved it can serve it: an accelerator measured on what the stream needs (for example HDR tone mapping, or HEVC output), or the processor. The processor and the accelerators are two separate pools, and a stream on the graphics card still spends a little processor for its audio and packaging.

When room runs short, the server answers in this order:

  1. A lower quality. A new stream whose tallest quality does not fit is admitted at the tallest one that does, and that ceiling holds for the whole stream.
  2. The processor. When the accelerators are full, a new stream moves to the processor if it has room.
  3. A refusal. When neither has room, the player shows The server is busy transcoding other streams and can retry.

A graphics card encode that fails on one title sends that title to the processor for a while, for every viewer. The card itself is set aside only after a test encode independent of the media fails on it too, and is tried again later: see Hardware acceleration.

While someone watches, the server's own background work (thumbnails, intro detection, media analysis) pauses, so that playback keeps the machine: see Background work and server load.

When one kind of source keeps making viewers wait despite all this, the server lowers its maximum quality for a while, then lifts the limit on its own. See Monitoring and logs.

docs.title: What is encoded
docs.text: Default Video codec H.264. HEVC when the player decodes it and a graphics card encodes it, or when the profile's Preferred Video Codec asks for it; AV1 when enabled (AV1 output, hardware only) and the player decodes it. Resolution The source's, unless a limit applies: the player's maximum, the bitrate limit, or what the server can encode in real time. Bitrate Follows the source, scaled to the resolution. Video bitrate ceiling caps it; Video bitrate ceiling, remote viewers caps it lower outside the local networks. Audio AAC. See Audio. Delivery HLS, in fragmented MP4 segments. The two ceilings of Admin → Transcoding: for every viewer, and for viewers outside the local networks.

docs.title: The transcoding cache
docs.text:
Encoded segments are kept on disk in the evey-cache volume and reused when another viewer, or the same one later, plays the same title with the same decision. Admin → Transcode Cache shows its size and clears it; the Transcode cache budget (Admin → Server Config → Server Settings) caps it.

Tip

Clear the cache after an update that changes how videos are encoded, so that nobody is served segments from the previous version. Clearing it while someone watches makes their stream rebuffer once, then resume.

docs.title: Checking what happens
docs.text:
• Admin → Now Playing: every stream, its method track by track, and the backend encoding it.
  • Admin → Transcoding → Encode calibration: the measured ceilings and the accelerators in use.
  • Admin → Streaming Quality: how playback went for real viewers.
  • Load test (Admin → Transcoding): simulates viewers to measure what the server sustains. It refuses to run while anyone is watching.

docs.title: Watching together
docs.text: How to watch the same title at the same moment as other people, each on their own device, and what each of you can expect to control. For viewers; nothing to configure on the server. Watch Together opens a room that holds the position, and every player follows it. Each viewer's stream is still decided for their own device, as in How playback is decided: one person can be in Direct Play while another is transcoded.

docs.title: Starting and joining a room
docs.text:
Web Android Android TV Start a room Watch Together in the player Watch Together in the player - Join with an account The room's link, or the code in Listen Together → Join a room The code in Listen Together The code in Settings → Watch Together Join without an account Watch together on the sign-in page, with the code Same -

The person who starts the room is its host and sees its code: six characters, letters and digits. Codes are typed without worrying about case, spaces, or confusing O with 0 and I or L with 1.

Joining with an account follows the usual rules: the library must be shared with that account, and the profile's parental settings must allow the title. A restricted profile cannot open a room on a title it may not watch either.

docs.title: What each member controls
docs.text:
Host Other members Android Play, pause and seek move the whole room. Play, pause and seek stay on your own screen. Android TV Play and pause move the whole room; a seek stays on the TV. Same as Android. Web Play, pause and seek stay on your own screen, for the host too. Same.

In the web player, explicit buttons replace the host's control. Sync everyone brings the whole room to your position and resumes playback; any member can use it, not only the host. Catch up brings you back to where the room is, without moving anyone else; it is offered on the guest page (joined with a code, without an account), not in the signed-in player.

Someone who joins late starts where the room is now, not where it was when the last command was sent.

If the host leaves, the member who has been in the room longest becomes the host. When the last member leaves, the room closes, and the guest access its code gave is withdrawn. A room nobody ever entered is removed after an hour.

docs.title: Guests without an account
docs.text:
A guest who enters a code on the sign-in page watches that one title and nothing else:

  • streaming only, never downloading;
  • video rooms only, not music rooms;
  • the access lasts while it is used, lapses after three hours without playback and after 24 hours in any case, and ends as soon as the room closes.

Warning

The code is the only thing that protects a room, so share it only with the people you want in it. Wrong codes are limited per address and across the whole server, which keeps guessing them out of reach.

docs.title: Listening together
docs.text: A music room is started from Listen Together with a queue of albums, tracks and playlists. The host plays, pauses, and moves through the queue; every member follows. Guests without an account cannot join music rooms.

docs.title: Plugin API reference
docs.text: The contract a plugin is written against: the fields of plugin.yaml, the two gRPC services the backend and the server exchange, and the window.evey bridge an interface module gets in its frame. The walkthrough that uses them is Writing a plugin; what each permission allows and what the installer refuses is in Permissions and slots.

docs.title: Manifest
docs.text:
Every ZIP carries a plugin.yaml (or plugin.yml) at its root, 1 MB at most.

plugin.yaml
name: my-plugin              # required; unique, kebab-case
version: 1.2.3               # required; semver, X.Y.Z or X.Y.Z-label
kind: plugin                 # required; "plugin" or "theme"
language: nodejs             # required for a plugin; a runtime of the image
entrypoint: node index.js    # required for a plugin; the command line the server runs

description: "..."           # optional
author: "..."                # optional
min_evey_version: "1.0.0"    # optional; recorded, not enforced today

permissions:                 # what the backend and the interface may call
  - network
  - media.read
external_fetch:              # required with "network"; bare hostnames only
  - api.themoviedb.org
capabilities:                # the roles the plugin says it fulfils
  - metadata.provider

web_root: public/            # required when frontend is declared; served as static assets
frontend:
  - slot: home.section       # one of the allowed slots
    src: public/front.js     # must be under web_root

config_schema:               # the fields of the Config panel on the plugin's card
  api_key:
    type: password           # never sent back to any client
    label: API key
    required: true
  city:
    type: string
    default: Paris
    description: Resolved through geocoding
Field Rule name, version, kind Required. version must match X.Y.Z or X.Y.Z-label; an update must carry a higher version than the installed one. language Required for kind: plugin: python, nodejs, php, ruby, lua, bash, sh or go. It picks the runtime check and the stubs copied next to the entrypoint; it does not launch anything. entrypoint Required for kind: plugin. The first token is the interpreter (or the binary, with native-binary), the rest its arguments; the process runs in the plugin's directory. permissions Each value must be in the permissions catalog. network requires a non-empty external_fetch. external_fetch Bare hostnames. A scheme is tolerated and dropped; a wildcard or an IP literal refuses the install (rules). capabilities metadata.provider, media.read, media.write, webhook.receiver or notification.sender; anything else is refused. A theme may declare none. web_root Required when frontend is non-empty; relative, no .., no backslash. . serves the whole plugin directory and only logs a warning. frontend[] slot must be in the slot list; src must be under web_root. config_schema A map of field name to {type, label, description, required, default, min, max, options}. Types: string, text, password, boolean, integer, number, select (with options: [{value, label}]).

A theme (kind: theme) must not declare language, entrypoint, permissions or capabilities; its format is in Themes.

Secrets. A field of type: password, or with secret: true, is stored and handed to the backend as usual but comes back masked from every read route, the admin Config panel included. Saving the panel with the mask unchanged keeps the stored value, so editing another field never wipes a secret.

docs.title: Backend: the two services
docs.text:
The backend process and the server speak gRPC over two Unix sockets whose paths arrive in the environment:

EVEY_PLUGIN_ID=<plugin id>
EVEY_PLUGIN_SOCK=<path>   # your process listens here and serves PluginService
EVEY_HOST_SOCK=<path>     # your process dials here to call HostService

The server authenticates the process on its socket by the PID the kernel reports (SO_PEERCRED); no token is handed to the process. Calls are limited to 600 per minute per plugin. proto/plugin/v1/plugin_api.proto is the contract; stubs for the bundled languages are copied next to the entrypoint when the plugin starts (prerequisites).

docs.title: PluginService: what the server calls
docs.text: Method When Initialize(plugin_id, config, host_version) Once the process has bound its socket. config carries the values of config_schema the administrator set. Answer success: false with an error to refuse to start. HealthCheck() Periodically, to tell a live process from a hung one. Answer healthy: true while you can serve. Shutdown(reason) When the plugin is disabled, updated, uninstalled or the server stops. Exit soon after answering. OnEvent(event_type, payload, source) Defined in the contract, but the server delivers no event to plugins today: implement it to answer handled: true, and expect no call. GetCapabilities() Defined in the contract; the server does not call it today.

docs.title: HostService: what the plugin can call
docs.text:
A call whose permission the manifest does not declare is refused with PermissionDenied. Methods marked not served answer Unimplemented; they are part of the contract for a later version and are listed so that a stub does not mislead you.

Method Permission Notes Log(level, message, fields) none Written to the plugin's log, shown under Logs on its card. GetConfig(key) / SetConfig(key, value) none The plugin's configuration: the values from the Config panel, plus keys the plugin writes itself. At most 256 keys, keys of 256 bytes, values of 16 KiB. GetData, SetData, DeleteData, ListDataKeys none The data store below. EmitEvent(event_type, payload) none Published on the server's event bus as plugin.event.<event_type>, where webhooks can subscribe to it. GetMediaItem(id), ListMediaItems(library_id, type, parent_id, limit, offset) api.library or media.read The full media record, including file_path, provider_ids and genres. Fetch(url, method, headers) network The only way out of the sandbox: http or https, GET or HEAD, a host of external_fetch, private addresses refused after resolution and through redirects. The body is capped at 8 MiB (truncated says so) and the whole request at 20 seconds. The server attaches no credential of its own. SearchMedia, GetMediaStreams, GetChapters, GetSubtitles api.library or media.read Not served. UpdateMetadata api.metadata or media.write Not served. GetUserPreferences api.user Not served. SendNotification notification.sender Not served.

docs.title: Data store
docs.text:
Every plugin owns a persistent key/value store, with no permission to declare: cursors, caches, a last-sync timestamp, anything to remember across restarts. Values are opaque strings; encode JSON yourself. The plugin id comes from the authenticated socket, so a plugin reads and writes its own namespace only, and the whole store is deleted with the plugin.

Method Purpose SetData(key, value) Create or replace a value. GetData(key) Returns value and found. DeleteData(key) Remove a key. ListDataKeys() The plugin's keys.

This store is global to the plugin. Data per user (a preference of the person looking at the widget) lives on the interface side, through the prefs permission below.

docs.title: Frontend API
docs.text: An interface module runs in a frame with an opaque origin, under a policy of default-src 'none': no access to the host page, its cookies or its storage, no form, no popup, and a connect-src limited to the hosts of external_fetch over https. Everything else goes through window.evey, injected before the module runs. The same module runs unchanged in the web app and in the mobile and television apps.

docs.title: evey.onInit(callback)
docs.text:
Called once with the context the host sends; a callback registered after the context arrived is called immediately.

evey.onInit(function (data) {
  // data.context         - the plugin's config values (config_schema)
  // data.locale          - the active locale, e.g. "en-US"
  // data.theme           - the active theme id
  // data.surface         - "web", "mobile" or "tv"
  // data.suggestedHeight - home.section only: the height (px) the host recommends
  // data.viewportHeight  - tv only: the panel height in dp
});

docs.title: evey.navigate(path)
docs.text: Moves the host application to path. Only /home, /library, /media, /player, /settings and /search prefixes are followed; anything else (the admin area, sign-in, an absolute URL) is dropped silently.

docs.title: evey.toast(level, message)
docs.text: Shows a toast in the host interface. level is "success", "error" or "info"; message is plain text, cut at 200 characters; at most 3 toasts per second are shown.

docs.title: evey.resize(height)
docs.text: Asks for the slot to be height pixels tall, clamped between 50 and 800. 0 collapses the slot: a widget with nothing to show takes no room. A home.section widget opens at data.suggestedHeight without doing anything: the host knows the surface it put you on and recommends the height a home widget has there, so every widget lands the same size. Resize only when you know better.

docs.title: evey.prefs.* (permission prefs)
docs.text:
The current user's preferences in the plugin's own namespace, bound to (this plugin, this user) by the token the host holds for the frame. Each call returns a promise; a missing permission rejects it.

await evey.prefs.set("units", "celsius");
const { value, found } = await evey.prefs.get("units");
const all = await evey.prefs.list();        // [{ key, value }]
await evey.prefs.delete("units");

docs.title: evey.media.* (permission public)
docs.text:
A safe projection of media items: id, title, type, year, overview, poster URL. Never a file path, a size, a provider id or a stream.

const item  = await evey.media.get(id);
const page  = await evey.media.list({ libraryId });
const data  = await evey.media.poster(id);  // the poster as a data: URL

poster returns a data: URL because the frame's policy forbids loading an image from the server directly; use it as an <img> source or a texture.

docs.title: evey.assets.read(path)
docs.text: Reads one of the plugin's own web_root files, by relative path, as a data: URL: a file the backend wrote at run time becomes usable in the frame without a cross-origin concern. Only the plugin's own assets are reachable.

docs.title: On a television
docs.text:
The television app runs the module in a WebView, and a few things that are true in a browser stop being true there:

  • Do not size from your own viewport. Inside the WebView, window.innerHeight is the slot the host just granted you. Size from data.viewportHeight or data.suggestedHeight.
  • No focus, no pointer. The widget never receives the D-pad focus and there is no hover; anything interactive belongs to the web and mobile surfaces.
  • Keep text away from the edges. Televisions overscan: leave about 5% of the width and height free on every side.
  • Test WebGL on a real box. A shader runs on the box's GPU and driver, not on your desktop's; keep noise coordinates bounded. tests/plugins/weather-v2 is the reference widget for all of the above.

docs.title: Slots
docs.text:
Slot Where it appears home.section A content section on the home page home.hero The hero banner area of the home page library.sidebar A sidebar panel in library views media.detail.sidebar A sidebar panel on a media detail page player.overlay An overlay layer on the video player settings.user.appearance The appearance section of the user settings sidebar.bottom The bottom of the main navigation sidebar admin.nav One entry in the admin menu, opening the plugin's own page

admin.nav is the only admin-area slot. It injects nothing into existing admin screens: it adds a menu entry that opens the plugin's page in the same sandboxed frame, on an admin-gated route. Asking for it shows in the consent diff. Every other admin.*, login.*, setup.* and profile.security.* slot is refused at install.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text: A capability declares the role the plugin says it fulfils: metadata.provider, media.read, media.write, webhook.receiver or notification.sender. The installer checks the name, the administrator sees the list in the preview and any addition at update, and the Security Dashboard records it. The server does not route anything on a capability today: a metadata.provider receives no enrichment call, a webhook.receiver receives no inbound request. What a plugin can actually do is decided by its permissions.

docs.title: Permissions of the interface
docs.text:
public and prefs are declared under permissions like the others. They grant nothing to the backend process; they unlock evey.media.* and evey.prefs.* in the frame. The frame never holds a token: the host mints a five-minute token scoped to (plugin, user) and proxies the calls, and the server refuses by default every method the token's scopes do not name (ADR-0012).

What a plugin can never ask for

admin.*, auth.*, system.*, user.write and library.write are hard-locked: a manifest that names them is refused, a token can never carry them, and admin methods refuse a plugin token whatever its scopes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: examples/plugins/ holds working plugins in the current manifest format: starters in Node.js and Python (nodejs-example, python-example), a metadata provider (metadata-example), a webhook receiver (webhook-receiver), a home widget with a build step (weather), the data store with the public and prefs permissions and the admin.nav slot (data-demo), a tour of every config_schema field type (config-demo), and two themes (theme-dark-blue, open-workshop). make plugin-zips packages them all.

docs.title: Writing a plugin
docs.text:
This page takes a developer from a clone of Evey to a plugin running on a local server, then to a signed package other administrators can install. The tutorial in section 3 is the happy path; the rest is reference you will come back to. The calls and fields themselves are in the Plugin API reference.

flowchart LR
  subgraph server["Evey server"]
    host["HostService<br/>checks every call against<br/>the declared permissions"]
    ui["Web interface<br/>plugin slots"]
  end
  subgraph plugin["Plugin, in its sandbox"]
    backend["PluginService<br/>your backend process"]
    front["Frontend module<br/>isolated iframe"]
  end
  backend <-->|"gRPC over a Unix socket"| host
  front <-->|"postMessage bridge"| ui
  host -->|"Fetch: declared hosts only"| net(("Internet"))

A plugin is a ZIP with a plugin.yaml at its root and a backend process the server starts in a sandbox. The process serves a small gRPC service on a Unix socket and calls the server back on another one. It may also ship an interface module, drawn in a sandboxed frame of the page, and talk to the outside world only through the server, to the hosts it declared.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Tool Why Go 1.27, Node.js 22 with pnpm, Docker with Compose The dev stack (make dev) builds the server and the web app. bubblewrap (bwrap) Only for the bubblewrap and strict sandbox modes. The default auto mode uses Landlock and needs nothing on a kernel 5.13 or later. cosign To sign your package before distributing it (section 7). Not needed to develop.

Pick the language of your plugin from the runtimes the server can start: python, nodejs, php, ruby, lua, bash and sh need their interpreter in the image, go ships a compiled binary and needs the native-binary permission. The default image carries Python only; the -nodejs image adds Node.js and the -full image adds PHP, Ruby and Lua. A manifest that names a runtime the image lacks is refused at install, with the list of the runtimes available.

The gRPC contract is one file, proto/plugin/v1/plugin_api.proto. Stubs are generated for Python, Node.js, PHP, Ruby, Dart, Java and Swift under sdk/<language>/, and the server copies the stubs of your language next to your entrypoint when the plugin starts, so a Node.js or Python plugin has nothing to vendor: the image provides @grpc/grpc-js and @grpc/proto-loader to Node.js plugins and grpcio to Python ones. For another language, generate stubs with protoc and ship them in the ZIP:

protoc --proto_path=proto \
       --<lang>_out=OUT_DIR --grpc_<lang>_out=OUT_DIR \
       proto/plugin/v1/plugin_api.proto

make plugin-sdk regenerates the shipped stubs; each sdk/<lang>/README.md names the gRPC plugin its language needs.

docs.title: 2. Bring up Evey locally
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:Evey-project/evey.git
cd evey
cp .env.dev.example .env.dev   # then set MEDIA_DIR, EVEY_DB_PASSWORD, MEILI_MASTER_KEY
make setup                      # once: adds evey.test to /etc/hosts
make dev                        # postgres, meilisearch, the server (Air), the web app (Vite)

Open https://evey.test. The setup wizard creates the administrator account on first launch, as described in First setup. Plugin files land in ./evey-data/plugins/<plugin-id>/, mounted as /data/plugins in the container.

docs.title: 3. Your first plugin, step by step
docs.text:
The example examples/plugins/nodejs-example is the smallest complete plugin: it serves PluginService, dials HostService, and writes a line in its log when the server starts it. We copy it, change one thing, and install it.

  1. Copy the example.

    cp -r examples/plugins/nodejs-example ~/hello-plugin
cd ~/hello-plugin

  2. Give it a name. Edit plugin.yaml:

    plugin.yaml
    name: hello-plugin          # unique, kebab-case
kind: plugin
version: 1.0.0              # semver: bump it at every upload
description: Says hello in its log
author: you
language: nodejs            # the runtime the server must have
entrypoint: node main.js    # the command line the server runs
permissions:
  - api.library             # lets the backend read media items

    language tells the server which runtime to check and which stubs to copy; entrypoint is what it runs, in the plugin's directory, with the environment of the next step.

  3. Read main.js. The server passes three variables to the process: EVEY_PLUGIN_ID, EVEY_PLUGIN_SOCK (the socket your process must listen on, serving PluginService) and EVEY_HOST_SOCK (the socket you dial to call HostService). The example loads plugin_api.proto from its own directory, where the server copied it, and implements the five methods of PluginService. Change the message in Initialize:

    main.js (excerpt)
    Initialize(call, callback) {
  hostLog("LOG_LEVEL_INFO", `hello from ${process.env.EVEY_PLUGIN_ID}`);
  callback(null, { success: true });
},

  4. Zip it. The manifest must sit at the root of the archive, not in a sub-directory:

    zip -r ../hello-plugin.zip . -x ".*" "node_modules/*"

  5. Install it. In Admin → Plugins, Install Plugin, choose the ZIP and Preview & Install: the preview lists api.library and the result of the static analysis. Through the API, the same upload is:

    curl -F "plugin=@hello-plugin.zip" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $EVEY_TOKEN" \
     https://evey.test/api/v1/admin/plugins/upload

  6. Read the log. On the plugin's card, Logs shows the line written by Initialize. docker compose logs evey carries the server side of the same start, under the plugin's id.

  7. Iterate. Change the code, bump version, zip again and use Update from source… on the card. An upload with the same or a lower version is refused; a new permission in the manifest triggers the consent step the administrator must approve.

What you have is the whole backend contract. From here, a plugin grows in three directions: calling the server (HostService, section 4), drawing an interface (section 5), and reaching the outside world (section 6).

docs.title: 4. Call the server from the backend
docs.text:
Every HostService call carries the plugin's identity: the server checks the process on the socket by its PID, and an interceptor refuses any call whose permission the manifest does not declare. Three groups need no permission at all:

  • Log writes to the plugin's log, shown on its card;
  • GetConfig reads the values the administrator set in Config (declared in config_schema), SetConfig lets the plugin keep its own keys there;
  • GetData / SetData / DeleteData / ListDataKeys is the plugin's private key/value store, wiped at uninstall.

GetMediaItem and ListMediaItems need api.library or media.read; Fetch needs network. The full table, with the methods declared in the contract but not served yet, is in the API reference.

docs.title: 5. Add an interface
docs.text:
An interface is a JavaScript module the page loads in a sandboxed frame, in one of the slots the server allows. Declare where the files are and where the module goes:

plugin.yaml
web_root: dist               # the directory served as static assets
frontend:
  - slot: home.section       # see the slot list
    src: dist/index.js       # must be under web_root

The module gets a window.evey bridge: evey.onInit hands it the plugin's config, the locale, the theme and the surface it landed on; evey.resize, evey.toast and evey.navigate act on the page within fixed limits; and, when the manifest declares prefs or public, evey.prefs.* and evey.media.* reach the server through a short-lived token the host holds for the frame. examples/plugins/weather is a complete widget with a build step; examples/plugins/data-demo shows prefs, public and the admin.nav slot. The bridge and the slots are described in the API reference.

docs.title: 6. Reach the outside world
docs.text:
A plugin process can open no socket to the internet, in any sandbox mode. The only way out is the Fetch call of HostService: the server checks the target against the manifest, then performs the request itself.

plugin.yaml
permissions:
  - network
external_fetch:
  - api.open-meteo.com       # bare hostnames: no scheme, no wildcard, no IP

network without external_fetch is refused at install. At run time the broker accepts http and https, GET and HEAD, answers up to 8 MiB within 20 seconds, and refuses private or reserved addresses even through a redirect. The frame of the interface gets the same host list as its connect-src, so a widget may call those hosts directly over https. The rules are in Permissions and slots.

Hosts are a contract with the administrator

The administrator sees the host list at install and must approve any addition at update. Keep it to what the plugin needs, and say in your README what each host receives.

docs.title: 7. Sign your plugin
docs.text:
What a signature proves

A signature says the ZIP the administrator installs is byte for byte the one you published, signed with the key they trust. It says nothing about what the plugin does: the permissions, the hosts and the analysis of the preview still apply. Evey checks it offline and in process (ECDSA P-256 over the SHA-256 of the ZIP, the format cosign sign-blob --key produces): no cosign binary on the server, no network, no transparency log.

You need cosign on your machine only.

  1. Once: generate a key pair.

    # choose a real passphrase; cosign.key stays private, never commit it
COSIGN_PASSWORD="your-passphrase" cosign generate-key-pair
# -> cosign.key (private) and cosign.pub (the file you hand out)

  2. At each release: zip, then sign the exact file you will distribute.

    cd hello-plugin && zip -r ../hello-plugin.zip . && cd ..

COSIGN_PASSWORD="your-passphrase" cosign sign-blob \
  --key cosign.key --tlog-upload=false --yes \
  --output-signature hello-plugin.zip.sig \
  hello-plugin.zip

  3. Check it before shipping, with the same verification the server does:

    cosign verify-blob --key cosign.pub --signature hello-plugin.zip.sig \
  --insecure-ignore-tlog hello-plugin.zip      # -> Verified OK

  4. Publish three files together: hello-plugin.zip, hello-plugin.zip.sig and cosign.pub. Put the public key's fingerprint somewhere your users can compare it (README, release notes), so they know cosign.pub was not swapped.

On the instance that installs it, the administrator sets the key and a policy and restarts the server:

EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY=/etc/evey/cosign.pub
EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_POLICY=warn   # or "enforce" to refuse what does not verify

Then, in Admin → Plugins, they choose the ZIP and, in Signature file (.zip.sig, optional), its .zip.sig; through the API, the signature is the sig field of the upload. The preview shows Signed or an invalid signature, and the Security Dashboard keeps the result.

Things that trip people up:

  • Any change to the ZIP breaks the signature, even re-zipping the same files. Sign the file you distribute, and sign again for every version.
  • Only ECDSA P-256 keys are accepted, which is what cosign generate-key-pair makes. Keyless signing and KMS references are not verified.
  • The key is read from a PEM file at startup: a missing or malformed file stops the server instead of failing the first install. With enforce and no key, the server refuses to start.
  • With the default warn and no public key configured, nothing is verified; the server only logs a warning at startup.
  • A wrong key, a tampered ZIP and a missing .sig all read as a failed signature: under enforce, the install or the update is refused.

docs.title: 8. What the installer checks, in order
docs.text:
Every step can refuse the package; the administrator sees the reason, and the server log carries the detail.

  1. Manifest. plugin.yaml is read straight out of the ZIP: required fields, semver, known permissions and capabilities, slots in the allowed list, external_fetch entries that are bare hostnames, web_root present when frontend is declared. The declared language must be a runtime of the image.
  2. Version and escalation. For a plugin already installed, the new version must be higher, and any new permission, capability, slot or host stops the install here until the administrator approves the difference (accept_permission_changes=true on the upload route).
  3. Signature and hash. The signature is verified when a public key is configured; a failure blocks only under enforce. The hash of the ZIP is recorded, and checked again when an update previewed earlier is applied.
  4. Extraction into a staging directory: at most 5,000 entries, 100 MB per file, 500 MB in total, a compression ratio of 100:1, no symbolic link, no path leaving the archive. An update never touches the running version until every later step passes.
  5. Themes only: the stylesheet is sanitized and written back, and a theme.js that matches a forbidden pattern refuses the package.
  6. Static analysis of every text file: a critical finding refuses the package; the deserialization and obfuscation warnings refuse it too, and native_code, compiled binaries and embedded archives refuse it unless the manifest declares native-binary.
  7. Persist and start. The staging directory is swapped into place, the row is written, and the process is started.

What the analysis looks for is listed in Plugin sandbox and threat model. It also reads comments: a # pip install foo line in a comment is reported like code.

docs.title: 9. What your process runs under
docs.text:
The server starts the process under a lower CPU priority, with a memory ceiling, a limit on processes and threads, and a size limit on its directory; a monitor stops a plugin that exceeds them. The defaults are 256 MiB, 64 processes and 100 MiB, adjustable by the administrator in Admin → Plugins → Resource limits. Without the subprocess permission, the process cannot spawn children, whatever the language; threads work.

The sandbox confines the filesystem to the plugin's directory and cuts every network socket, unconditionally. Which mode is in force depends on the host, not on the plugin: Plugin sandbox and threat model describes them, and Plugin sandbox setup tells an administrator which to pick.

docs.title: 10. Distribute a plugin
docs.text:
There is no catalog: an administrator installs a plugin by uploading its ZIP or pasting its URL in the admin panel, from wherever you publish it (a release on a forge, your own site).

  • Ship the ZIP, its .sig and your cosign.pub together (section 7).
  • State the permissions and the external_fetch hosts in your README: the administrator sees them at install and has to approve them; a surprise there is the first reason an install is refused.
  • To have your plugin listed with the bundled examples, open a pull request against examples/plugins/ with the source and a README. Examples are reviewed and built from source; a listing is not an endorsement and carries no signature from the project.

docs.title: 11. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix plugin requires "nodejs" runtime which is not installed in this image The image variant lacks the interpreter. Use the -nodejs or -full image, or write the plugin in Python. manifest: external_fetch entry "*.tmdb.org" is a wildcard - use explicit hostnames Wildcards are refused at install, no exceptions. List every hostname you need (api.tmdb.org, image.tmdb.org). manifest: frontend slot "admin.section" not allowed The slot is outside the allowed list. Pick a slot from the slot list; admin.nav is the only admin-area slot. manifest: network permission requires non-empty external_fetch network declared without hosts. Add the hosts, or drop the permission. plugin already installed at version 1.0.0, new version must be higher The ZIP carries the installed version. Bump version, or uninstall first. signature does not match the plugin or the configured key The .sig was made with another key, or the ZIP changed after signing. Re-sign the exact ZIP with the right key, or fix EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY. plugin blocked: theme.js contains forbidden pattern The theme script scanner matched a banned API. A theme may only call evey.theme.*: see Themes. The log ends with memory quota exceeded (... MB > ... MB) The monitor stopped the plugin past its memory limit. Lower memory usage, or raise Max memory (MiB) in Resource limits. bwrap: ... permission denied bubblewrap mode inside Docker, blocked by the container's seccomp or AppArmor profile. Keep the default auto mode. Otherwise see Plugin sandbox setup. The interface module does not appear The plugin is disabled, the slot is misspelled, or src is not under web_root. Check the card's state, the slot name, and the /api/v1/plugins/<id>/assets/... requests in the browser's network panel.

docs.title: Plugin sandbox setup
docs.text: Which sandbox setup fits your server, in plain words. For almost everyone the answer is: leave the defaults. The server detects the machine and picks the strongest isolation it can. Read on only if you run an old NAS, run Evey without Docker, or want to tighten things further. The full technical model is in Security model and plugin sandbox.

docs.title: What protects you
docs.text:
A plugin you install is boxed in. Depending on the machine, the box:

  • limits which files it can touch: its own folder and the system libraries it needs, nothing else (not your media, not your secrets, not other plugins);
  • blocks dangerous system actions at the kernel: debugging other processes, loading modules, changing the clock, mounting disks;
  • cuts off direct network access, always: a plugin that asked for the network, and that you approved, reaches only the hosts it declared, through the server;
  • caps CPU, memory, disk and process count, so a runaway plugin cannot take the server down;
  • keeps your secrets unreadable: the login-signing key and the backups.

On top of that, plugins are admin-only to install, scanned for suspicious code, and you approve their permissions before they run.

Check what is in force: Admin -> Plugins -> Security Dashboard shows the host sandbox, the mode auto resolved to (landlock, bubblewrap or basic) with the probe results (Landlock kernel, Sandbox launcher, Bubblewrap). basic means the host offers no per-path file isolation: plugins run with a uid drop and seccomp only, the probes say why, and the sections below say what to change.

docs.title: Pick your situation
docs.text: Your server What you get out of the box Anything to do? Modern Linux in Docker (kernel 5.13 or newer, roughly anything from 2021 on), the normal case the strongest isolation (Landlock), automatically nothing Old NAS in Docker (kernel older than 5.13) good isolation minus the per-folder file walls; secrets, network and system actions stay locked down nothing: uid separation (below) turns itself on Any Linux, no Docker the strongest isolation available: Landlock on a modern kernel, otherwise bubblewrap namespaces follow Without a container

docs.title: The one knob you might touch: uid separation
docs.text:
Uid separation makes a plugin run under a different user account than the server, so it physically cannot read the server's secret files even if nothing else stopped it. It only matters on a machine without the per-folder file walls (the basic case); on a modern machine the walls already keep secrets out of reach, and the separation is a redundant extra layer.

EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION:

Value Meaning Use it when auto (default) on only when it is needed (the basic case), off where it is redundant always, unless one of the two cases below applies on always on, a second independent wall on top of the file walls you want belt and braces and accept the small cost below off never a specific plugin misbehaves when run under it (rare)

Warning

Uid separation is incompatible with the no-new-privileges Docker option: pick one. When the drop cannot be granted on an old machine (basic), the server refuses to start the plugin rather than run it next to your secrets; on a modern machine it logs a warning and runs the plugin without the extra wall. The image ships everything needed, you only set the variable.

The small cost of on: the plugin runs as a separate account, so a plugin that writes scratch files inside its own folder can trip up. If one does, set off. That is why the default is auto: it only takes that risk where there is a real benefit.

docs.title: What a malicious plugin could do
docs.text:
Modern Linux (Docker or bare metal): a bad plugin is fully boxed in. It cannot read your secrets, cannot see or touch other plugins' files, cannot make arbitrary network calls and cannot tamper with the system. The only realistic way out is a serious kernel bug, true of any sandbox that is not a full virtual machine.

Old NAS in Docker, no per-folder walls (basic):

  • your secrets stay protected (login key, backups) by the separate user account, which auto turns on here;
  • the plugin has no direct network; a permitted one reaches only the hosts it declared;
  • dangerous system actions are still blocked at the kernel;
  • but with no per-folder walls, a bad plugin could read ordinary, non-secret files, list running processes and, because plugins share one account, read or disturb another plugin's files.

Only install plugins you trust on such a host, or move to a modern kernel for the full file walls.

docs.title: Configuration examples
docs.text:
These go in your .env (compose) or as EVEY_* environment variables.

1. Modern server, recommended (nothing to do)
EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=auto          # picks the strongest available (default)
# EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION=auto      # (default) on only where needed
2. Old NAS (nothing to set, shown for clarity)
# keep no-new-privileges out of the compose security_opt, it would block the drop
EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=auto
EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION=auto        # (default) on in the basic case
3. Belt and braces on a modern server
EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=auto          # resolves to landlock
EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION=on          # add the independent uid wall on top
4. Pin a mode (advanced)
EVEY_PLUGINS_SANDBOX_MODE=landlock      # refuse to start plugins if Landlock is unavailable
5. A plugin breaks under uid separation
EVEY_PLUGINS_UID_SEPARATION=off
6. Resource caps (editable later from Admin -> Plugins -> Resource limits)
EVEY_PLUGINS_MEMORY_MB=256              # max RAM per plugin
EVEY_PLUGINS_PIDS_MAX=64                # max processes and threads
EVEY_PLUGINS_DISK_MAX_MB=100            # max install-dir size (0 = off)
EVEY_PLUGINS_CPU_NICE=10                # scheduling priority 0-19 (higher = nicer)

docs.title: Change the sandbox mode while running
docs.text: Change Sandbox mode in the Resource limits card of Admin -> Plugins. Running plugins are restarted automatically so the new mode takes effect at once, and the Security Dashboard shows the mode in force. A plugin that cannot run under the new mode (for example bubblewrap inside an unprivileged container) shows up as errored: switch back.

docs.title: Verify it is working
docs.text:
# the launcher carries the capability used for uid separation
docker exec evey-server getcap /evey-plugin-launcher        # cap_setuid=ep

# which user a running plugin runs as (evey = shared with the server,
# evey-plugin = separated); the image has no ps, so ask Docker
docker top evey-server -o user,pid,args | grep -iE "node|python"

The sandbox mode in force is the badge of Admin -> Plugins -> Security Dashboard.

docs.title: Permissions and slots
docs.text: For plugin authors: what a manifest may declare, what the installer checks, and the rules that apply to a plugin at run time. The catalog below is the list to pick from; how the server contains a plugin, and what that containment cannot stop, is described in Plugin sandbox and threat model.

docs.title: What is checked at install
docs.text:
A plugin is refused at install when:

  • kind is missing, or is neither plugin nor theme;
  • a kind: plugin lacks language or entrypoint, or a kind: theme declares them, or declares permissions or capabilities;
  • a permission or a capability is unknown;
  • a frontend module targets a slot outside the slot list;
  • an external_fetch entry breaks the fetch rules, or network is declared without any entry;
  • the ZIP breaks the extraction limits;
  • the static analysis finds a critical pattern, or a warning the installer treats as one (unsafe deserialization, obfuscation). Compiled binaries, embedded archives and native code are refused unless the manifest declares native-binary.

The analysis also reads comments: a # pip install foo line in a comment is reported like real code. Remove such lines before publishing. The categories are listed in Plugin sandbox and threat model.

Before installing, the administrator sees the declared permissions, slots and hosts, and what the analysis found. Nothing a plugin declares is granted silently.

docs.title: What the plugin runs under
docs.text:
Whatever the manifest declares:

  • the plugin sees its own directory, not the server's data;
  • it has no direct network access: a plugin with the network permission reaches the hosts of its external_fetch list through the host's Fetch call, and nothing else;
  • without subprocess, it cannot start child processes (threads work);
  • it runs under resource limits the administrator can adjust: 256 MiB of memory, 64 processes and threads, 100 MiB of disk for its directory, and a lower CPU priority by default.

Signing is optional during development. How to sign a plugin, and the signature policy a server can enforce: Writing a plugin.

docs.title: Permissions catalog
docs.text:
A permission is declared under permissions; any other value refuses the install. Receiving webhooks (webhook.receiver) and providing metadata (metadata.provider) are capabilities, declared under capabilities: see Plugin API reference.

Permission What it grants network The backend may call Fetch. Must be combined with a non-empty external_fetch list; refused at install without it. The process itself still has no socket. subprocess The backend may spawn child processes. Without it, the launcher's kernel filter refuses fork, vfork and clone without CLONE_THREAD, and the seccomp shim refuses execve for interpreted plugins. Threads keep working either way. The administrator sees a dedicated warning. native-binary The package may ship .so, .dll, .exe, .wasm, .jar, embedded archives or native code the analysis cannot read. The administrator sees and must accept opaque code. Required for a go plugin. filesystem Declared intent to touch the filesystem beyond the plugin's directory. Recorded and shown to the administrator; the sandbox grants no file access outside the plugin's directory whatever is declared. media.read GetMediaItem and ListMediaItems on the host: the full media record. media.write Reserved for the metadata write calls, not served today. api.library The same media read calls as media.read. api.user Reserved for GetUserPreferences, not served today. api.metadata Reserved for UpdateMetadata, not served today. notification.sender Reserved for SendNotification, not served today. public The interface may read a safe projection of media items (id, title, type, year, overview, poster), never paths or streams. See evey.media.*. prefs The interface may read and write the current user's preferences in the plugin's own namespace. See evey.prefs.*. hardware.gpu The process gets the host's DRM render node (the real renderD1xx, never a card node). A kernel-driver attack surface and a GPU-memory boundary shared with the transcoder: a hung GPU can stall transcoding. Without it, GPU nodes are excluded from the Landlock allowlist entirely; with it, the launcher adds an IOCTL_DEV rule scoped to that one file (Landlock ABI 5 or later; on older kernels, read and write access alone permits command submission). The preview shows a critical warning. Grant it only to plugins you would run outside a sandbox.

docs.title: External fetch rules
docs.text:
Declared in external_fetch: [...] and checked at install (validateExternalFetch). All-or-nothing: one invalid entry refuses the whole install.

An entry is a bare hostname. A scheme prefix is tolerated and discarded; only the hostname is kept.

Entry Valid Reason api.tmdb.org Yes Exact hostname, the normal form https://api.tmdb.org Yes Scheme parsed and dropped, hostname kept *.tmdb.org No Wildcards are refused: list every subdomain you need * No Same rule 192.168.1.1, ::1 No IP literals are refused, both families

At run time the host broker adds its own limits, which the manifest cannot widen: http and https only, GET and HEAD only, the target host matched case-insensitively against your list (a :port suffix in an entry is ignored), private or reserved addresses refused after DNS resolution, a body capped at 8 MiB and a request at 20 seconds. Redirects are re-checked against both the list and the address rule.

The same host list is the connect-src of the plugin's frame, prefixed with https://: a widget may call those hosts directly, over https only.

docs.title: Slot whitelist
docs.text:
Plugins may inject UI only in explicitly allowed slots. Critical paths are intentionally absent.

Slot Auth required Notes home.section Yes Main page content area home.hero Yes Hero banner area library.sidebar Yes Library view sidebar media.detail.sidebar Yes Media detail sidebar player.overlay Yes Player overlay UI settings.user.appearance Yes Appearance section in user settings sidebar.bottom Yes Bottom area of the navigation tray admin.nav Yes One nav entry in the admin panel opening the plugin's own sandboxed page; it does not inject into existing admin screens

Never allowed: admin.* (except admin.nav), login.*, setup.*, profile.security.*. These paths are authentication- or privilege-critical, and injection there is a privilege-escalation or phishing vector.

admin.nav content is sandboxed like any other slot: it renders in an <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts"> without allow-same-origin, in a page whose policy is default-src 'none', so it is third-party content displayed in the admin area, not an admin capability granted to the plugin.

The bridge limits what a frame can ask of the page: evey.toast at most 3 messages per second, 200 characters, no HTML; evey.navigate only /home, /library, /media, /player, /settings and /search; evey.resize clamped to 50-800 px. The frame holds no token: the host mints a five-minute token scoped to (plugin, user) for the public and prefs calls, and the server refuses by default every method that token does not name.

docs.title: Update workflow
docs.text:
1. The administrator uploads a new ZIP. PreviewPluginUpdate runs the static analysis and the signature check and returns the difference in permissions, capabilities, slots and external_fetch against the installed version.
  2. If the difference is not empty, the administrator must acknowledge it before the update is applied (requires_ack = true; through the upload route, accept_permission_changes=true).
  3. The hash of the package is captured at preview and verified at apply: the ZIP that was analysed is the ZIP that gets installed.
  4. Under EVEY_PLUGINS_COSIGN_POLICY=enforce, a signature failure at the apply step blocks the update even if the preview passed.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: The server binary doubles as the operator's command line: evey admin <subcommand> runs one maintenance or recovery tool against the same configuration and database as the server, then exits. This page lists the commands and how to run them in the container; the day-to-day procedures (lost password, key rotation, restore) are in Recovery.

docs.title: Running a command
docs.text:
In the standard installation, the commands run inside the container, which already carries the database password and the EVEY_* configuration:

docker exec evey-server evey admin doctor
docker exec -it evey-server bash      # an admin shell: evey admin ..., man evey

On an install without Docker, the binary is called directly (evey admin reset-password --user alice@example.com); it reads the same EVEY_* variables as the server (EVEY_DB_HOST, EVEY_DB_USER, EVEY_DB_PASSWORD, EVEY_DB_NAME, EVEY_BACKUP_DIR...). Most commands need the database; none starts the server, and most are safe to run while it is stopped.

Invocation What it does evey Starts the server. evey admin <subcommand> Runs one operator tool and exits. evey admin alone prints the list and exits 1; evey admin <subcommand> --help details one. evey version Version, commit, build date. Needs no configuration or database, so it answers from a container that will not start. evey help The command summary. evey man [--text] The manual: roff for man, plain text with --text. evey completion bash The bash completion script.

Any other first argument is refused (exit 1) rather than silently booting the server.

docs.title: The commands
docs.text: The list below is the binary's own --help text, grouped as evey admin prints it. evey admin with no subcommand is always the current list.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
evey admin reset-password --user <email>     Generate a new password for the user, print it once.
                                             Every session of that user is ended at the same time.
evey admin rotate-jwt-key                    Regenerate the JWT signing key. Invalidates ALL active
                                             sessions: the key is moved aside (kept as
                                             <key>.rotated-<timestamp>), the next server boot
                                             generates a new one, and every session is ended in the
                                             database at once.
evey admin restore-backup <path-to-dump.sql.gz>
                                             Restore the database from a pg_dump.gz file, in a single
